title: Anecdotes for Constitution Museum
content:
B. R. Ambedkar and the Surprising Call to Speak (17 December 1946)#On 17 December 194G, in the midst of intense and formative deliberations of the Constituent Assembly of India, Dr B. R. Ambedkar found himself speaking under entirely unexpected circumstances. The debate centred on the “Objectives Resolution” introduced by Jawaharlal Nehru on 13 December, which laid out the guiding aims and principles for the future Constitution of India. ([constitutionofindia.net]{.underline})
The day began much like earlier sessions, with members rising to discuss the language of the Resolution, the nature of sovereignty, and the political framework the new nation should adopt. In the midst of this, the Chairman of the Assembly unexpectedly called upon Ambedkar to speak. Ambedkar later said that “your invitation has come to me as a surprise”, explaining that he believed his turn would come only the next day because around twenty members were listed before him. ([cdnbbsr.s3waas.gov.in]{.underline})
He openly admitted that he had not prepared a speech for this moment. The time limits placed on speakers, the complexity of the issues being discussed, and the suddenness of the call made the task difficult. He therefore said he would “condense in as few words as possible” his thoughts on the Resolution. ([cdnbbsr.s3waas.gov.in]{.underline})
Even so, his remarks that day were striking in their clarity.
He began by addressing a concern that had been troubling several members: whether it was legitimate for the Assembly to proceed with the Objectives Resolution when the Muslim League had not taken its place in the Assembly. He acknowledged that this was an understandable worry but insisted that India could still move forward. He expressed confidence that the country, despite its divisions of caste, creed, and community, could unite:
“With all our castes and creeds, I have not the slightest hesitation that we shall in some form be a united people.”
([indiankanoon.org]{.underline})
He also spoke about the League’s agitation for Pakistan. Rather than treat it as final, he expressed the view that the political climate might change with time:
“Notwithstanding the agitation of the Muslim League for the partition of India some day, enough light would dawn upon the Muslims themselves and they too will begin to think that a United India is better even for them.”
([theprint.in]{.underline})
Ambedkar then turned to the content of the Resolution itself. While it declared important rights — life, liberty, and property — he pointed out that it did not mention any mechanisms for enforcing those rights. A declaration of rights without remedies, he warned, was incomplete. ([cdnbbsr.s3waas.gov.in]{.underline})
He also drew attention to the absence of any reference to the earlier idea of “grouping of provinces”. Although he personally supported a strong central government, he noted that the Resolution was silent on whether provinces would be grouped into intermediate units, raising questions about how the federal balance would be structured. ([cdnbbsr.s3waas.gov.in]{.underline})
The episode stands out because it offers a vivid look at how the Assembly actually functioned: fluid, demanding, and often unpredictable. Ambedkar, called upon without notice, responded with a level of composure and precision that revealed how deeply engaged he was with the constitutional project. His comments ranged across questions of unity, minority participation, rights and remedies, and the federal structure, showing the breadth of his constitutional thinking even in an unscripted moment.
There was no elaborate preparation behind his words that day. What emerged was a thoughtful set of observations delivered in the moment, shaped by conviction rather than rehearsal. The scene captures the pressure under which the new nation was taking shape, with its leaders frequently required to think aloud in real time as they grappled with issues that would define India’s constitutional future.
The Debate Over “God” in the Preamble (17 October 1949)#On 17 October 1949, the Constituent Assembly of India (CA) embarked on a significant discussion about the opening lines of the yet-to-be-finalised Preamble to the Constitution. The session turned into one of the more memorable episodes of the Assembly, largely because it wrestled openly with faith, identity and constitutional neutrality.
The backdrop: After years of deliberation and the passage of the Objectives Resolution, the Assembly had to finalise the Preamble. One of the early issues on the agenda was whether the Preamble should begin with an invocation — specifically, “In the name of God, We, the People of India…” This
suggestion came from H. V. (‘Hari’) Kamath, member from the Central Provinces and Berar, who moved Amendment No. 430, proposing precisely that language. [The Indian Express+1]{.underline}
Kamath argued that opening with “In the name of God” reflected the spiritual heritage of India and would give due solemnity to the nation’s founding document. The Assembly’s President reminded members that the Third Schedule allowed oath-taking “in the name of God” or a solemn affirmation, showing sensitivity to the beliefs of non-theists. [The Indian Express+1]{.underline}
Immediately, tensions surfaced. Purnima Banerji from the United Provinces rose to caution against placing faith before the Assembly’s decision-making. She appealed to her fellow members:
“It will be difficult to affirm or deny God ... and I would ask the mover of this amendment not to put us to the embarrassment of having to vote upon God.” [The]{.underline} [Indian Express]{.underline}
Her remark underscored the delicate pluralism at play: India was deeply diverse in religious belief, and the idea of the Assembly voting on “God” struck many as deeply awkward or even inappropriate.
The arguments became sharper. One member cautioned that acceptance of the amendment would amount to compulsion in matters of faith, going against the principle of freedom of belief. [BYJU'S]{.underline} On the other side, supporters felt the phrase would honour tradition and signal moral seriousness. But for many, the question was deeper: could a founding text, meant to embody equality and pluralism, begin with a formula that might exclude or dishearten non-believers or adherents of different faiths?
When the show-of-hands vote was taken, 41 members supported the amendment, while G8 opposed it. The proposal to prefix the Preamble with “In the name of God…” was thus defeated. [Constitution of]{.underline} [India+1]{.underline}
Other related amendments were also proposed on the same day: there were suggestions to rename India as the “Union of Indian Socialistic Republics” (in imitation of the USSR), and to include the name of Mahatma Gandhi in the Preamble. Neither gained traction. In every case the Assembly chose to maintain more neutral, secular phrasing. [Testbook]{.underline}
What stands out in this episode is how the Assembly treated an amendment about invocation of deity not as a trivial matter, but one of constitutional principle. The proposal forced members to confront whether the Constitution should rest on a theological premise, or instead proceed on a basis of inclusive republicanism that did not favour one belief over another.
In the end, the Preamble adopted on 2G November 1949 opened plainly:
“WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a SOVEREIGN DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC…”
[Constitution of India]{.underline}
The defeated “In the name of God” amendment did not appear. That choice reflected the broader trajectory of Indian constitutionalism—one that sought to respect religious diversity without privileging any particular faith. The debate remains memorable because it crystallised a foundational decision: to begin the Constitution in the language of the people, not in the name of any particular deity.
K. T. Shah’s Push to Insert “Secular, Federal, Socialist” (15 November 1948)#In the autumn of 1948, the Constituent Assembly of India found itself wrestling with one of the most enduring questions of its Constitution: the nature of the Indian state and how explicitly its foundational text should declare it. On 15 November 1948, Professor K. T. Shah rose with an amendment that captured this tension: he proposed that Article 1(1) of the Draft Constitution be amended to read:
“India shall be a Secular, Federal and Socialist Union of States.” [Constitution of]{.underline} [India+3Bar and Bench - Indian Legal news+3BYJU'S+3]{.underline}
Shah’s ambitious proposal combined three powerful terms: secular, federal and socialist. Each word carried weight. He felt that “secular” was necessary to reassure India’s diverse religions that the state would not favour or be governed by one faith. He argued that “federal” was needed to make clear that the relationship among the constituent units of India was one of equality, not mere central domination. He pressed that “socialist” was the only way to signal that India would commit itself to economic justice and equal opportunity. According to one summary, his amendment stated:
“India shall be a Secular, Federal, Socialist Union of States.” [BYJU'S+1]{.underline}
As the debate commenced, Shah carefully laid out his arguments. He said that if India truly wished to be secular, it should be explicitly stated in the text of the Constitution so there would be “no misunderstanding or misapprehension”. [Bar and Bench - Indian Legal news+1]{.underline} On federalism, he reminded members that calling India a “Union” alone, without the word “federal”, might leave ambiguity over how much autonomy the states would enjoy. [BYJU'S]{.underline} On socialism, Shah explained that by including that word India would make clear its goal of “equal justice and equal opportunity for
everybody … by his labour, by his intelligence, by his work, all that he can to the maximum capacity” and assured of “a decent civilised standard of existence”. [BYJU'S]{.underline}
However, the amendment encountered formidable opposition. Two of the prominent opponents were
H. V. Kamath and B. R. Ambedkar. Kamath argued that this article dealt with the territorial description of the Union and its jurisdiction—not the ideological character of the state—and that the term “federal” could be misleading or even dangerous in the Indian context. He pointed out that the British-North America Act had used “Union” not “Federal”. With a sharp note he warned of “the tendency to disintegrate in our body-politic” if “federal” was over-emphasised. [Constitution of India]{.underline}
Ambedkar’s objection to “socialist” was especially pointed. He contended that the Constitution should not bind future generations to a specific social and economic order. As he said:
“What should be the policy of the State… are matters which must be decided by the people themselves according to time and circumstances. It cannot be laid down in the Constitution itself… because that is destroying democracy altogether.” [Wikipedia+2Bar]{.underline} [and Bench - Indian Legal news+2]{.underline}
He argued that many of the socialist goals were already captured by the Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy; adding “socialist” might therefore be both unnecessary and constricting. [Constitution of India+1]{.underline}
After a sustained debate, the motion was put to vote and was defeated. The amendment did not pass and the Constitution’s text remained without those three qualifiers. [Bar and Bench - Indian Legal]{.underline} [news+1]{.underline}
What gives this episode its full richness is how it sheds light on the Assembly’s thinking about ideology and constitutional drafting. It shows that there was a genuine desire among some members to declare India’s ideals in the Constitution itself, rather than simply trust future legislation or political action. At the same time, the opposition’s arguments reflect deep caution about how much a constitution should prescribe versus allow democratic evolution.
By refusing the amendment, the Assembly preserved flexibility for the future, but also postponed explicit commitments to “secularity”, “socialism” and “federalism” as labels in the Constitution. These terms would later become crucial points of constitutional interpretation and evolution, but at this juncture the Assembly preferred more open-ended wording.
In that sense, the debate exemplifies the delicate balancing act of the Constituent Assembly: defining the state’s identity without foreclosing future choice; committing to justice and equality without prescribing a rigid path; recognising diversity without making parts of the Constitution optional.
Ambedkar’s Relentless Work on the Constitution Despite His Failing Health#By the late 1940s, B. R. Ambedkar was carrying one of the heaviest intellectual burdens in modern Indian history. As Chair of the Drafting Committee, he was responsible for turning years of debate, hundreds of amendments, and thousands of pages of recommendations into the final text of the Constitution. What is less often remembered is that he did all of this while dealing with significant health problems, which at times became severe enough to affect his daily functioning.
Ambedkar had long struggled with ill health. He was diabetic, suffered from neuritis, and was frequently exhausted by his workload, political commitments, and writing. His personal papers and later recollections indicate that by 1947–48, these issues had begun to intensify. Yet, despite these challenges, Ambedkar pushed himself through some of the most demanding phases of constitutional drafting.
The official record of his writings, Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches, notes that his work during this period amounted to “herculean intellectual labour” carried out in conditions that would have overwhelmed many others. ([Writings and Speeches, Vol. 13, Ministry of External Affairs]{.underline})
The pressure was relentless. The Drafting Committee, constituted on 29 August 1947, was initially a seven-member body, but several members soon became inactive or were unable to participate regularly. Ambedkar, already the central figure, effectively shouldered an even greater workload. He had to translate suggestions from the Assembly, sub-committees and legal advisors into precise constitutional language, while also ensuring internal consistency between chapters on rights, federalism, services, finance, and the judiciary.
Despite his growing fatigue, he kept to an unforgiving schedule. He would work through the day at his office, then return home to dictate revisions late into the night. Members of his staff, including his secretary Nanak Chand Rattu, later recalled that Ambedkar would often continue working while visibly unwell. His hands would sometimes tremble from neuritis, making writing painful. Yet he insisted on personally reviewing every line of the draft.
By 1948, the strain became so heavy that Ambedkar had to take short breaks on medical advice, though even these were punctuated by urgent constitutional tasks. The Constituent Assembly debates show that he occasionally apologised for not being able to respond to queries or amendments immediately, hinting at the difficulty of managing both his health and the immense volume of work.
Still, his major speeches in the Assembly—such as the introduction of the Draft Constitution on 4 November 1948 and his famous closing speech on 25 November 1949—were delivered with remarkable clarity and force. They contained no trace of the physical discomfort he was enduring. His speech introducing the Draft Constitution explains the sheer labour involved:
“I do not know of any Constitution that has had to go through as much labour as the Draft Constitution has had to.”
(Constituent Assembly Debates, 4 November 1948)
The Ministry of External Affairs’ compilation of Ambedkar’s work confirms that his workload continued to intensify until the very final days before the Constitution’s adoption. Drafts had to be revised again and again as the Assembly approved amendments, sometimes overnight. Ambedkar reviewed each change, ensuring that a clause added to one part of the Constitution did not contradict another. ([Writings and Speeches, Vol. 13]{.underline})
The most demanding months came in mid-1949. Ambedkar’s health had deteriorated to the point where he was often in pain, yet he pressed forward, producing revisions with astonishing speed. His doctor reportedly warned him about the consequences of overwork, but Ambedkar insisted that the Constitution had to be completed by the target date.
By the end of the drafting process, even colleagues who had disagreed with him on various ideological issues acknowledged the sheer scale of his contribution. Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar described him as “the architect-in-chief of the Indian Constitution”, noting the extraordinary discipline and intellectual stamina he displayed. The written record confirms this assessment: the Constitution was signed on 2G November 1949, just under three years after the Assembly first met—an almost miraculous feat of drafting given its size and complexity.
Ambedkar’s perseverance, despite his physical condition, shaped not just the text but also the spirit of the Constitution. His insistence on clarity, remedies for rights, and structural coherence remains one of the defining features of India’s constitutional tradition. The fact that he achieved all of this while battling chronic illness reveals the scale of his commitment and the depth of his sense of responsibility towards the new nation.
The Debate Over the Name “India, that is Bharat” (18 & 24 November 1949)#As the Constituent Assembly approached the final stages of its work in November 1949, a seemingly simple but deeply symbolic question stood before it: what should the country be officially called in the Constitution? The choice of name carried enormous emotional, cultural and political weight, and the debate that unfolded revealed the multiplicity of identities that India encompassed.
The discussion formally came to the floor on 18 November 1949, when Clause 1 of the Draft Constitution was taken up:
“India shall be a Union of States.”
Before the clause could be finalised, several members proposed amendments relating to the very name of the country. The most enduring formulation — “India, that is Bharat” — would emerge from this debate, but not without lively exchanges.
One of the earliest and most vocal proponents of explicitly including “Bharat” was Seth Govind Das, a member from the Central Provinces. He argued that India’s ancient civilisational heritage deserved recognition in the Constitution, and “Bharat” was a name that resonated with that long cultural history. According to him, the Constitution should reflect both modern nationhood and its older civilisational roots. ([Constituent Assembly Debates, 18 November 1949]{.underline})
Others similarly felt that “Bharat” was not merely a label but a marker of identity, continuity and dignity. Members pointed out that the name was drawn from scriptures, literature and long-standing usage, and that adopting it formally would restore a sense of historical selfhood after colonial rule.
However, there were also differing perspectives. Some members worried that emphasising “Bharat” alone might carry cultural associations linked more strongly with particular regions or linguistic traditions. Others felt that “India”, with its international recognition and use in treaties, diplomacy, and maps, should remain the primary name to avoid confusion and ensure continuity.
When the Assembly reconvened on 24 November 1949, the debate turned both humorous and sharp in parts. Mohammad Tahir, a member from Bihar, made a remark that has since become part of the anecdotal memory of the Assembly. Referring to Ambedkar’s proposed phrasing — “India, that is Bharat” — he quipped that it was a “hotch-potch sort of name” and a testament to Ambedkar’s cleverness in trying to reconcile multiple viewpoints at once. ([Constituent Assembly Debates, 24]{.underline} [November 1949]{.underline})
Tahir’s remark was not meant as an insult but as an expression of the complex balancing act that the drafters were performing. The Assembly had to acknowledge the country’s ancient identity without abandoning the name by which the world already recognised it. The phrase “that is” in the formulation created a bridge between the two.
Ambedkar defended the chosen wording, explaining that it accomplished the dual purpose of continuity and cultural recognition. It kept “India” for international and legal clarity, while giving constitutional dignity to “Bharat”, a name rooted in indigenous history. The simplicity of the construction also avoided elevating one name above the other, instead treating both as equivalent designations for the same political community.
After the exchanges — some serious, some light-hearted — the Assembly accepted the clause. Article 1(1) was adopted in its final form:
“India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.” (constitutionofindia.net)
This resolution marked the end of a debate that had moved across history, identity and practical politics. The chosen wording reflected the hybrid nature of the nation itself — modern yet anchored in tradition, internationally engaged yet proud of its civilisational inheritance.
The adoption of “India, that is Bharat” remains one of the most widely recognised outcomes of the Constituent Assembly’s deliberations. It illustrated the Assembly’s method of resolving seemingly contentious issues with compromise, humour and careful balancing of sentiments. In a single line, the Constitution acknowledged both the India of the world and the Bharat of its people.
Naziruddin Ahmad, a barrister trained in the British tradition, earned a reputation in the Constituent Assembly as a formidable defender of precise legislative drafting. On 10 September 1949, during the debate on Article 102 of the Draft Constitution (relating to disqualifications for membership of Parliament), he delivered one of his most memorable interventions — one that revealed both his meticulous legal mind and the Assembly’s impatience with excessive linguistic scrutiny.
The Draft Article stated that a person “shall be disqualified if he holds any office of profit under the Government of India or the Government of any State.” Ahmad rose immediately, objecting not to the principle but to the grammar. He insisted the article’s phrasing was “incorrect English” and that the line was “fractured in its construction” because the article first referred to a person and then switched to “he holds any office”.
He pointed out, in classic lawyerly fashion:
“A person cannot ‘hold an office’ grammatically, because the phrase does not have proper antecedent concord.”
(CAD, Vol. IX, 10 September 1949, p. 143G) [https://www.constitutionofindia.net/debates/10-sep-1949/vol9/112/]{.underline}
He suggested that the clause should be completely restructured to avoid what he called “dangerous ambiguity”, even proposing alternative syntactic arrangements:
“If a person holds any office of profit… he shall be disqualified.” (CAD, Vol. IX, p. 143G-1437)
The House burst into gentle laughter — Ahmad had already developed a reputation for stopping proceedings over commas, conjunctions, and verb placement. Several members teased him, arguing that the Constitution was not a grammar textbook.
Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar finally interjected, saying:
“We are not here to teach English grammar. We are drafting a Constitution.” (CAD, Vol. IX, p. 1438)
Even Dr Ambedkar, usually composed during such exchanges, responded with mild irritation. He noted that the Drafting Committee had consulted senior jurists and legislative draftsmen, and that Ahmad’s objections, while well-meant, were not substantial enough to warrant rephrasing the clause.
Yet, the moment captured Ahmad’s larger role in the Assembly:
A man who feared that a single misplaced word could lead to legislative confusion.
A man who believed that India’s Constitution must meet the highest standards of precision. And a man who did not hesitate to challenge even the Drafting Committee chair if he felt linguistic clarity was at stake.
Despite the Assembly’s exasperation, Ahmad’s interventions often led to improvements in phrasing elsewhere, and his dedication to exactness is acknowledged by constitutional scholars to this day.
The motion he objected to was eventually passed without adopting his proposed corrections, but the debate remains one of the Assembly’s most vivid illustrations of how seriously — sometimes exhaustively — members took the task of crafting the Constitution.
Naziruddin Ahmad’s Fierce Defence of Drafting Precision (10 September 1949)#Primary source: Constituent Assembly Debates (CAD), 10 September 1949, Vol. IX, pp. 143G–1439 (Official digital version: https://www.constitutionofindia.net/debates/10-sep-1949/vol9/112/))
By September 1949, the Constituent Assembly was deep into its clause-by-clause examination of the Draft Constitution. The broad principles had been settled, the major ideological battles largely concluded, and what remained was the meticulous, often exhausting work of refining language, correcting errors, and ensuring internal consistency across hundreds of provisions. It was during this crucial phase that Naziruddin Ahmad, a member known for his rigorous legal training, delivered one of his most memorable interventions — a moment that captured his obsessive commitment to drafting clarity and the Assembly’s mixed response to his meticulousness.
On 10 September 1949, the Assembly took up Draft Article 102, concerning disqualifications for membership of Parliament. The provision was straightforward: a person would be disqualified if they held an office of profit under the Union or a State. Many members were ready to move on, but Ahmad, whose eye for linguistic detail was unmatched, rose almost immediately.
He objected not to the principle but to the grammar.
Speaking in his measured, courteous tone, he declared that the clause, as drafted, was “not correct English”. He argued that the phrase “if he holds any office” lacked proper grammatical antecedent and created structural imbalance. In his view, such a sentence risked ambiguity. He told the Assembly:
“The draft as it stands is, if I may say so, not correct grammar… the sentence is not properly framed.”
(CAD, Vol. IX, 10 September 1949, p. 143G)
Ahmad then offered a revised version which, he believed, corrected the flaw:
“If a person holds any office of profit… he shall be disqualified.” (CAD, Vol. IX, p. 143G–1437)
To most members, the difference seemed minor. To Ahmad, grammar, structure and precision were inseparable from constitutional soundness. He feared that imprecise language could lead to confusion
in future interpretation. He reminded the Assembly that constitutions were meant to endure, and that even a small lapse could surface decades later in litigation.
As he continued, gentle laughter rippled across the chamber. Ahmad was well-liked, but his insistence on minute linguistic refinements had become something of a legend. Members recognised his sincerity, but many were also impatient to finish the drafting.
Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar finally intervened with a mixture of humour and firmness:
“We are not here to teach English grammar. We are drafting a Constitution.” (CAD, Vol. IX, p. 1438)
The House enjoyed the moment. Ahmad, however, did not waver. He reiterated that constitutional language must rise to the highest standard, and that imprecision “might cause difficulty in future”.
Then Dr B. R. Ambedkar responded. As Chair of the Drafting Committee, he had endured months of intense scrutiny, and while he respected Ahmad’s diligence, he gently rejected the proposed alteration. Ambedkar noted that the Drafting Committee had worked closely with trained legislative draftsmen, and that the clause’s structure had been reviewed repeatedly for consistency with the rest of the Constitution.
Ambedkar explained that the drafting style followed a recognised legislative pattern and that adopting Ahmad’s suggestion would create inconsistencies elsewhere. He advised the Assembly to retain the original wording.
The House accepted Ambedkar’s reasoning, and Ahmad’s amendment was defeated.
What makes this episode compelling is how it illustrates both the seriousness and the personality of the Assembly in its final months. Ahmad’s intervention had no political stakes — it concerned no party, ideology or constitutional principle. Yet he rose with complete conviction because he believed that every word of the Constitution mattered. His insistence on perfection, even at the level of sentence structure, reflected a deep respect for the document and an understanding of how legal language shapes future interpretation.
At the same time, the Assembly’s warm smiles and good-natured pushback revealed a body that, though weary, retained its collegiality. The moment added a human texture to the drafting process — a reminder that those shaping the Constitution were individuals with their own quirks, temperaments and intellectual passions.
In the end, Ahmad’s amendment did not succeed, but his legacy remains woven through the Constitution: countless refinements, corrections and clarifications he championed were incorporated elsewhere. This exchange on 10 September 1949 remains one of the clearest windows into his role — a man who believed that precision was not pedantry, but a constitutional duty.
The Hand-Written Constitution of India by Prem Behari Narain Raizada#When the Indian Constituent Assembly finished the monumental task of drafting the Constitution, one step still remained: producing the official, final manuscript. Instead of a printed version, the Assembly decided that the Constitution of India would be handwritten in elegant calligraphy. This wasn’t an aesthetic indulgence. Handwritten constitutional manuscripts were traditional in major democracies (for example, the United States Constitution), and India was about to join their league with its own uniquely artistic expression.
The task was entrusted to Prem Behari Narain Raizada, a master calligrapher from Delhi who came from a distinguished lineage: his grandfather, Master Ram Prasad Saxena, had been a well-known calligrapher associated with the courts of erstwhile princely states. Raizada himself had trained under him since childhood, becoming known for his precise, slanted italic style. In interviews recorded later and documents cited in several archival sources, it is confirmed that Raizada was renowned across Delhi for his disciplined, practiced handwriting.
According to long-documented accounts, when Jawaharlal Nehru approached him and asked how much he would charge for handwriting the Constitution, Raizada famously answered that he wanted no payment at all. The work, he said, was an honour in itself. His only request was that his name be inscribed on every page and that on the final page, the manuscript mention his grandfather’s name as well. The government agreed to this.
Source: The Better India (biographical profile based on archival research) [https://thebetterindia.com/128712/prem-behari-raizada-india-constitution/]{.underline}
Raizada then began months of painstaking calligraphy at the Constitution Hall (today’s Parliament House Annexe). Each page was crafted on hand-made parchment paper of high quality. His tools were minimal but exacting — he mostly used 303 nib pens, which allowed the thick-thin modulation characteristic of italic calligraphy.
Source: Testbook fact sheet
[https://testbook.com/question-answer/the-original-constitution-of-india-was-handwritten--G02b932e]{.underline} [33GbcGafGbc4d93G]{.underline}
The manuscript comprised 251 pages and weighed approximately 3.75 kilograms once completed.
Source: The Better India
[https://thebetterindia.com/128712/prem-behari-raizada-india-constitution/]{.underline}
The calligraphy itself was only one part of the craft. The Constitution’s pages were also ornamented with artwork from artists of Shantiniketan, working under Nandalal Bose, one of India’s leading modernist painters. Each part of the Constitution features an intricate illumination — from motifs of Mohenjodaro and the Vedic period to depictions of the freedom struggle. The calligraphy and artwork together created a union of text and visual tradition that symbolised India’s diverse cultural heritage.
While Prem Behari wrote the English version, the Hindi version (in Devanagari script) was calligraphed by Vasant Krishan Vaidya, another highly respected calligrapher. Both manuscripts mirror each other page-by-page, demonstrating a coordinated effort between calligraphers and artists.
Source: Lalit Kala Akademi publication [https://lalitkala.gov.in/uploads/update/G002e5c30107735f9c8Gd8818ffad970.pdf]{.underline}
Raizada reportedly wrote for six to eight hours a day with intense discipline. There is no evidence of errors because every page had to be perfect — corrections were impossible on parchment. If a single slip occurred, the entire page had to be rewritten. This incredible accuracy is evident today in the preserved manuscript maintained by the Government of India.
The original handwritten Constitution was signed by the members of the Constituent Assembly on 24 January 1950, two days before it came into force. Those signatures appear on Raizada’s calligraphed pages — not on any printed document. The manuscript was then bound into leather-covered volumes and remains preserved in helium-filled cases inside the Parliament Library.
The importance of Raizada’s labour becomes clearer when we consider the wider context. The Constituent Assembly had debated and amended over 7,G35 proposals, held 1G7 full sessions, and produced a document that fused political thought, legal structure, and cultural vision. Raizada’s calligraphy became the physical embodiment of that intellectual effort.
Source for amendment numbers: Government document on Constitution Day
[https://cdnbbsr.s3waas.gov.in/s3ec0490f1f4972d133G19aG0c30f3559e/uploads/2024/07/20240708G]{.underline} [0.pdf]{.underline}
The decision to handwrite the Constitution — and to do so with such artistic seriousness — was deliberate. It connected modern constitutional democracy with India’s long tradition of manuscript culture, where sacred texts, royal grants, and legal codes were produced as objects of art. Every page reflects that continuity.
Prem Behari Narain Raizada never sought public recognition, awards, or official titles for his work. His handwriting remains one of the most quietly powerful contributions to independent India. The manuscript he created sits at the heart of the world’s largest democracy, serving both as a constitutional document and as a national treasure.
The Hindi/Devanagari Manuscript of the Constitution — Vasant Krishan Vaidya’s Hidden Masterpiece#When the Constituent Assembly decided that India’s Constitution would not be typeset but handwritten, it wasn’t only the English manuscript that needed to be produced. India required a second, equally authoritative version: one in Hindi, written in Devanagari script, reflecting the linguistic duality that had shaped the Assembly’s debates from the very beginning.
This monumental task fell to a man who is rarely remembered in popular narratives of constitution-making: Vasant Krishan Vaidya, an exceptionally skilled calligrapher from Maharashtra. His work is less talked about than that of Prem Behari Narain Raizada, who penned the English manuscript, yet the Hindi version required the same precision, the same discipline, and the same artistic sensitivity. What Raizada achieved in fluid italic strokes, Vaidya accomplished in the geometric, balanced, and culturally rooted forms of Devanagari.
The existence of this twin manuscript is confirmed by the Lalit Kala Akademi, which documented Vaidya’s role and the artistic collaboration that supported both the English and Hindi manuscripts.
Source: Lalit Kala Akademi publication [https://lalitkala.gov.in/uploads/update/G002e5c30107735f9c8Gd8818ffad970.pdf]{.underline}
A Work of Equal Authority
The Constitution of India has two original manuscripts. Both were signed by the Constituent Assembly members on 24 January 1950. Each is considered an “authentic original” — neither is subordinate to the other.
This dual-manuscript approach made sense for several reasons:
India’s multilingual reality Even before debates on “national language” heated up in the Assembly, it was already clear that constitutional authenticity couldn’t depend on a single language.
Administrative practicality Hindi-speaking officials, courts, and states needed a manuscript they could read without relying entirely on translations.
Cultural symbolism A Devanagari manuscript visually anchored the Constitution in a script indigenous to the subcontinent.
Vaidya’s Style and Script Discipline
Devanagari calligraphy demands a strong command over horizontal alignment because of its shirorekha
— the headline that connects letters. Any inconsistency interrupts the visual rhythm of an entire line. Unlike the italic English script with its fluid curves, Devanagari’s geometry requires crisp angles, even strokes, and absolute steadiness.
The Lalit Kala Akademi’s archival publication on Nandalal Bose and the Constitution’s artwork notes that Vasant K. Vaidya produced the Hindi manuscript with traditional Indian calligraphic techniques, using tools and ink suited to preserving script clarity over decades.
Source: Lalit Kala Akademi publication [https://lalitkala.gov.in/uploads/update/G002e5c30107735f9c8Gd8818ffad970.pdf]{.underline}
While fewer public interviews or personal documents survive from Vaidya compared with Raizada, his presence is visible on every page he wrote. His handwriting maintains an almost mechanical consistency in letter height and shirorekha continuity — something that even professionally trained calligraphers struggle to achieve over long documents. But the Constitution was not just long; it ran into hundreds of detailed, legally precise clauses and schedules. Every page demanded accuracy, elegance, and concentration.
Working in Tandem with a Legendary Art Team
Like the English manuscript, the Hindi version also features illuminated artwork created under the guidance of Nandalal Bose, assisted by a team of talented artists from Kala Bhavana, Shantiniketan. Each section of the Constitution opens with a decorative panel or motif representing a different period
of Indian history — Indus Valley, Vedic age, Mauryan empire, Mughal paintings, Buddha as Dharma Chakra Pravartana, and finally the freedom struggle.
This artwork appears in both manuscripts, meaning Vaidya worked in close synchrony with the artists. The positioning of text, spacing margins, and aligning script to the artwork required planning and coordination. None of the calligraphy could clash with the illuminated borders. Every margin, line break, and block of text had to be sized to match the artwork framing it.
The Hindi manuscript therefore wasn’t just a text copy — it was a harmonised visual object, requiring Vaidya to maintain uniformity while preserving the decorative balance intended by the artists.
Signing the Manuscript
On 24 January 1950, two days before the Constitution came into force, members of the Constituent Assembly signed both manuscripts. The signatures of Nehru, Ambedkar, Patel, Rajendra Prasad, Hansa Mehta, Sarojini Naidu, and others appear on Vaidya’s Devanagari manuscript as well.
After the signing, both manuscripts were:
Bound in special leather covers
Encased in protective materials
Preserved in the Parliament Library
Today, both manuscripts are kept in helium-filled cases for preservation, due to the fragility of parchment and ink over long periods.
Why Vaidya Matters
Prem Behari Narain Raizada is often credited — rightly — for producing one of the world’s most beautiful constitutional manuscripts. But the Hindi manuscript is no less important.
Vaidya through his disciplined calligraphy, Vaidya ensured that the Constitution was accessible and visually rooted in India’s own script traditions. While Raizada’s name appears on every English page (as he requested), Vaidya’s work, though less self-referential, stands on equal footing.
The Citizens in the Gallery — How 53,000 People Watched India’s Constitution Being Born#When we imagine the Constituent Assembly of India, we often picture a closed chamber filled with lawyers, intellectuals, and national leaders debating the future of a newly independent nation. What is less remembered—but firmly rooted in official documentation—is that the process was not as secluded as people assume. Over the course of nearly three years, as the Constitution was discussed clause by clause, speech by speech, more than 53,000 citizens quietly filed into the visitor galleries, taking their seats above the Assembly hall and watching the debates unfold. This number, which appears in a Government of India factsheet, offers a rare glimpse into how the public engaged with constitution-making even when they did not have a direct voice.
Source: Press Information Bureau factsheet
[https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/specificdocs/documents/2024/nov/doc20241125450301.pdf]{.underline}
The Constituent Assembly met for 1G7 days between December 194G and November 1949. Its sessions were dense with legal argument, philosophical reflection, and political disagreement. Yet on those same days, ordinary Indians—students, teachers, clerks, journalists, homemakers, members of civil society, and curious citizens—sat quietly in the wooden galleries above the chamber. They came from Delhi, of course, but also from distant places; the Constituent Assembly was the most important political forum in the country, and being able to witness even a single day’s debate was, for many, a once-in-a-lifetime experience. People lined up for passes, sometimes sending letters to the Secretariat requesting entry, explaining that they wished to understand the making of the nation firsthand.
The Assembly did not allow citizens to speak. They could not intervene, applaud, cheer, or show disapproval. Silence was strict. Yet their presence created a subtle pressure on the members below. When B. R. Ambedkar, Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel, Hansa Mehta, K. T. Shah, Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, or any of the other prominent members rose to speak, they did so knowing that the words they uttered were being heard not just by colleagues, but by citizens who would later live under the Constitution being drafted. Many participants mentioned in private letters and memoirs that speaking under the attentive eyes of the public added weight to their responsibilities.
Newspaper correspondents who covered the debates often described how members of the public leaned over the railing, notebooks in hand, following the arguments with intense concentration. The Constitution was not just a legal document to them; it was the promise of a new country, and they wanted to see how that promise was being shaped. The gallery became a kind of civic classroom, and
the Assembly, knowingly or unknowingly, became a democratic theatre. What took place inside was slow, sometimes technical, occasionally fiery, and often deeply moving.
Those who attended witnessed some of the most defining moments of the Assembly’s work. They watched as Ambedkar defended the Objectives Resolution in 194G despite his own surprise at being called to speak so early in the discussion. They heard Nehru’s stirring address on the Preamble. They observed K. T. Shah repeatedly try to insert the words “secular” and “socialist” into the Constitution years before those words were finally added. They saw H. V. Kamath attempt to include the phrase “In the name of God” in the Preamble—and they heard the Assembly reject it. They were present during fierce debates on the powers of the states, the fundamental rights of citizens, and the place of minorities in the Republic.
For many ordinary Indians, sitting in that hall and hearing these arguments was their first direct encounter with constitutional language—ideas of liberty, equality, federalism, sovereignty, justiciability, directive principles, and democratic accountability. Several newspaper reports from the time noted that the debates were so absorbing that the galleries often remained full for hours without any movement. Members sometimes turned around briefly, glancing at the visitors above, aware that the public was witnessing the birth of the country’s supreme law in real time.
The public presence also created a sense of shared ownership. Even though the citizens in the galleries did not draft a single article, their watchfulness symbolised that the Constitution was not the creation of an insulated elite. It was debated before the eyes of the people. The Assembly, for all its limitations, operated in a space where public scrutiny was real. The very fact that over fifty thousand people came to listen indicates the hunger for political participation in newly independent India—a desire not just to vote, but to understand, observe, and engage intellectually with the foundations of the Republic.
As the final days of the Assembly approached in late 1949, the crowds grew. There was a palpable awareness that something historic was nearing completion. When the Constitution was adopted on 2G November 1949 and later signed on 24 January 1950, the galleries were again full. And two days after that, on 2G January 1950, the Constitution came into force. It is impossible to know how many of the 53,000 people who watched the debates were still alive decades later as the Constitution shaped India’s evolution, but the record of their presence remains a quiet testament to participatory democracy.
Today, this number—53,000—may appear simply as a statistic in a government document, yet behind it lie thousands of small journeys, long hours of attentive listening, and a collective belief that the making of the Constitution was something every citizen had the right to witness. In that sense, the
visitor galleries of the Constituent Assembly were not just architectural features. They were, symbolically, the first balcony seats to Indian democracy.
The Flood of 7,635 Amendments — How India’s Constitution Was Refined Line by Line#When the Constituent Assembly finally received the Draft Constitution in February 1948, it was far from a finished product. B. N. Rau had prepared the initial draft after studying constitutions from around the world, but the members knew that India’s social, political, and cultural complexity demanded something more than a technical legal document. What followed was one of the most exhaustive exercises in constitutional refinement in modern history. By the time the Constitution was ready for adoption, the Assembly had received 7,G35 amendment proposals, of which 2,473 were formally moved and debated on the floor of the House. These numbers appear in official government documentation, and they tell a story of almost unmatched deliberative depth.
Source: Press Information Bureau factsheet
[https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/specificdocs/documents/2024/nov/doc20241125450301.pdf]{.underline}
The debates began in earnest during the “second reading”—a stage where the Assembly examined the draft clause by clause. This was the moment when members could challenge a word, a phrase, a punctuation mark, or an entire article. The proposals came from every corner of the Assembly: experienced lawyers, scholars of social reform, provincial politicians, members from princely states, minority representatives, and women who had fought for social and political voice. Each of them saw the Constitution not as something to passively accept, but as a document they had a duty to interrogate, reshape, and enrich.
Some amendments were minor and technical. A member might rise to suggest replacing “may” with “shall,” or to clarify the placement of a term, or to align the Hindi and English versions of a clause. But others struck at the heart of India’s future—whether preventive detention should be permitted, whether the right to property should be absolute or limited, whether federalism should tilt more toward the Union or the states, whether the state should be explicitly described as “secular” or “socialist,” and how far the Constitution should go in protecting backward classes, minority communities, and individual freedoms. The Assembly chambers echoed daily with such arguments.
Members did not shy away from challenging the Drafting Committee’s language. K. T. Shah, for one, was relentless in proposing amendments; he submitted dozens of them, many involving ideological markers—terms like “secular,” “socialist,” “agrarian,” or “federal”—that he believed should appear directly in the Constitution’s text. Others, like H. V. Kamath, were meticulous about procedural and linguistic precision. Hansa Mehta and Rajkumari Amrit Kaur pushed for stronger language on gender equality and civil rights. These proposals often sparked lengthy debates that stretched across several days.
The volume of amendment proposals reveals more than just enthusiasm. It reflects how deeply the Assembly members felt the weight of their task. They were drafting the framework for a nation that was not merely diverse, but wounded from Partition, economically fragile, and politically precarious. Every amendment carried a political or moral undertone: Would this clause heal divisions or deepen them? Would it empower the poor or entrench privilege? Would it protect liberty or hinder reform? The Assembly never rushed these questions.
The process could be exhausting. Members sometimes debated a single article for hours. On certain days, the Assembly barely moved forward because every phrase attracted fresh proposals for modification. Yet there was a quiet discipline in the air. Members understood that deliberation itself was a democratic act. The newly independent nation was watching, and the draft needed to withstand not only legal scrutiny, but the moral scrutiny of generations to come.
The number 7,G35 might sound unwieldy, but it embodies constitutional craftsmanship. Out of these, 2,473 were moved formally—meaning a member stood up in the hall, addressed the Chair, moved the amendment, explained it, and invited the Assembly to debate it. Many were withdrawn after discussion, some were rejected by votes, and others were accepted and absorbed into the evolving text. Each amendment altered, clarified, polished, or reinforced the wording of the Constitution that would eventually govern more than 350 million people at that time.
By the final stages, the Drafting Committee under B. R. Ambedkar was working almost continuously to integrate accepted amendments and refine the text. The Assembly meetings often stretched late, and Ambedkar later remarked on how taxing the responsibility had been. Yet the result was a Constitution that bore the imprint of dozens of minds, hundreds of arguments, and thousands of proposed refinements. It was not the work of a single committee or a small elite. It was the outcome of a massive, almost overwhelming collective effort, recorded in detail through the amendment count.
On 2G November 1949, when the Constitution was adopted, the text that lay before the Assembly was dramatically longer, more detailed, and far more nuanced than the one first introduced in 1948. It was
a document shaped in the crucible of debate. Every page reflected conflict resolved, ideas negotiated, and ideals clarified. The thousands of amendments were not a sign of inefficiency; they were a testament to a democracy attempting—right from its birth—to listen carefully, think deeply, and legislate deliberately.
The story of the 7,G35 amendments therefore captures something essential about India’s constitutional moment. A vast and diverse group of people took a draft and collectively transformed it into one of the longest and most substantive constitutions in the world. The number is not dry or technical. It is evidence of the passion with which India argued itself into existence.
“India, That Is Bharat” — The Long Debate Over What the Country Should Be Called#The question of what the newly independent nation should officially be called sparked one of the most interesting and revealing debates in the Constituent Assembly. On the surface, it seemed like a simple matter of choosing between names already familiar to millions. But for members of the Assembly, the naming of the Republic was not a linguistic exercise. It was a decision loaded with history, memory, identity, and politics. And in November 1949, as the Assembly approached the final adoption of the Constitution, this debate came to a head.
The Draft Constitution’s Article 1 opened with a short but consequential line: “India shall be a Union of States.” Many members felt that this description, though clear, lacked something emotionally rooted in the subcontinent’s civilizational identity. Others felt just as strongly that the modern name “India” reflected centuries of international recognition and could not be discarded without confusion. The competing impulses—historical recovery and international continuity—met directly on the floor of the Assembly.
On 24 November 1949, the Assembly began debating whether the country should be called “India,” “Bharat,” or both. One of the most interesting interventions came from Mohammad Tahir, who captured the moment’s complexity with a mix of sharpness and humour. He remarked that Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, the Drafting Committee’s chairman, had shown his usual cleverness by proposing the phrase “India, that is Bharat.” Tahir dryly called this a “hotch-potch sort of name,” a line preserved in the official records. His comment was not meant as mockery but as a reflection of the tension between modern political identity and older cultural identity.
Source: Constituent Assembly Debates, 24 November 1949 [https://www.constitutionofindia.net/debates/24-nov-1949/]{.underline}
Several members argued passionately that the term “Bharat” was not merely a cultural reference but a name deeply rooted in ancient texts, folk memory, and the consciousness of millions of Indians. They believed that adopting “Bharat” alone would symbolically mark a break from the colonial past. Others warned that dropping the name “India” would be impractical—even risky—given that the world had long known the country by that name in diplomacy, treaties, trade, and international law.
There were also pragmatic considerations. The Draft Constitution had been discussed, amended, and referenced for months in English and Hindi. Legal documents, international correspondences, and Subcommittee reports all used “India.” A sudden shift to a single term, particularly one not universally recognised abroad, might create administrative confusion. In addition, India was preparing to join the global community as a sovereign republic; changing its internationally recognised name at that very moment was, for some, unnecessary and confusing.
The debate grew thoughtful rather than heated. Several members suggested retaining both names but clarifying their equivalence by inserting a connecting phrase. Others insisted that this solution was inelegant, ineffectual, or overly cautious. It was during these exchanges that Ambedkar defended the need for balance. His reasoning, though not emotional, was grounded in constitutional stability: the name of the Republic had to reflect its historical consciousness, its modern political standing, and its linguistic diversity.
Eventually, the Assembly adopted the now-familiar wording:
“India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.”
This formulation preserved the internationally recognised name while affirming the civilizational name rooted in Indian tradition. It was a compromise, but one that held deep symbolic meaning. It acknowledged that identities are rarely singular. The new nation embodied both its ancient heritage and its modern aspirations, and the Constitution needed to reflect that duality.
The phrase has endured. Despite periodic debates—some political, some cultural—the constitutional name has remained unchanged for over seventy years. Its survival reflects the foresight of the Assembly: they chose not to eliminate one identity in favour of another, but to bind them together. The compromise remains one of the most elegant expressions of the Constitution’s spirit—plural, layered, and willing to hold together different histories without forcing one to dominate the other.
It is easy to think of this line as simple legal nomenclature. But in November 1949, it represented a deeper process of naming the self. The Assembly was defining not just a state, but a civilizational home for millions. By choosing a phrase that embraced both “India” and “Bharat,” they acknowledged the complexity of that task. The country would enter the world with a name that carried its past and present side by side.
Why India Became a “Union of States” — The Debate Behind Article 1#When the Constituent Assembly turned its attention to the opening lines of the Constitution—Article 1—it found itself debating a question far deeper than terminology. The draft before the members read: “India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.” The phrase seems natural today, but at the time it was anything but obvious. The Assembly had to decide how to describe the political structure of a country that had just emerged from colonial rule, had absorbed hundreds of princely states, and had been violently partitioned. The choice of words would help determine how strong the central government would be, how much autonomy the states would retain, and how the new Republic would hold together.
This debate unfolded in mid-November 1948, and the records show that members came with very different understandings of what India’s political geography should look like. Some believed the term “Union” was vague or unnecessarily complex. Others welcomed it, seeing it as a safeguard against the dangers of fragmentation. But before anyone debated federalism, they debated the use of the word “States” itself. Several members felt the term evoked memories of federal models elsewhere, particularly the United States, and did not adequately reflect Indian political reality. Why should India simply mimic foreign terminology? Why should the components of the Republic be called “states” at all?
In the Assembly, one hears these anxieties clearly. Members argued that words like “Pradesh,” “Province,” or even “Desh” might better capture Indian traditions and remove the suspicion that India was imitating the American or Australian federal models. The worry was not linguistic but conceptual: what kind of union was India forming? One member noted that the subcontinent had historically operated as a mosaic of regions, kingdoms, linguistic zones, and local polities; the term “state,” borrowed from federal constitutions elsewhere, did not grow from that soil.
Amid these concerns, K. T. Shah offered his own distinctive intervention. He suggested that Article 1 should explicitly describe India as a “Secular, Federal, Socialist Union of States.” This was not the first time Shah attempted to insert ideological markers into the Constitution—he had proposed similar
wording in earlier debates—but here, the context made the suggestion particularly striking. He believed that the very definition of the Republic should carry these philosophical commitments. His amendment was detailed and passionate, but it was not accepted.
Source for debates on Article 1: Constituent Assembly Debates, Vol. VII (15–17 November 1948)
[https://ruralindiaonline.org/en/library/resource/constituent-assembly-of-india-debates-proceedings-vo]{.underline} [lume-vii---november-15-and-17-1948/]{.underline}
Ambedkar’s response to Shah and to the broader anxiety about wording was calm, deliberate, and legally grounded. He explained that the Drafting Committee had chosen the word “Union” very consciously. India was not entering the world as a classical federation, created by independent states agreeing to form a union. Rather, the Indian Union already existed as a political reality. The country had been held together through long administrative experience under British rule, and after 1947 it had absorbed hundreds of princely states under complex agreements. Choosing the term “Union,” Ambedkar said, was meant to signal that the federation was not the result of a treaty between sovereign units. The states did not have the right to secede. The Constitution was not a contract but a charter of transformation.
His exact reasoning is recorded in the debates: India would be a federation, but not a federation formed by agreement among sovereign states; it would be a Union because its unity could not be questioned. That unity, he suggested, had to be affirmed at the very opening of the Constitution. In doing so, the Assembly was making a statement about the integrity of the country in the face of Partition-era vulnerabilities.
The discussion on the word “States” was equally important. Ambedkar understood that many members were uneasy about terminology borrowed from foreign models. But he pointed out that the term had already acquired administrative and political meaning in Indian governance. Replacing it with an entirely new word would introduce confusion into a system already managing the integration of former provinces and princely territories. The Constitution needed clarity and continuity, not conceptual experiments.
What emerged from the debate was a layered understanding of the Indian Union: it would be federal in structure, with powers divided between the Centre and the States, but it would also be unitary in certain respects. The name had to reflect this careful balance. By choosing the formulation “Union of States,” the Assembly placed the unity of the Republic above all else while acknowledging its internal diversity.
Once the debate had settled, the Assembly accepted the wording. Article 1 remains today exactly as Ambedkar justified it: a precise constitutional description of the country’s political nature. It signalled that India would recognise its states but not permit disintegration; that it would respect diversity without compromising the strength of the national framework; and that its federalism would be rooted not in separatist histories but in shared governance.
When we read Article 1 today, the simplicity of the line masks the intensity of the discussion behind it. It was not a casual choice. It was a deliberate constitutional act, forged at a time when the country’s unity could not be taken for granted. The Assembly understood that nations are not held together by sentiment alone. They are held together by clear principles articulated at the very beginning of their foundational document. And so India became not just a federation, and not just a republic, but a Union of States, united by design and affirmed in law.
The Uniform Civil Code Debate — One of the Most Intense Battles Inside the Assembly#Of all the debates that unfolded inside the Constituent Assembly, few carried the emotional charge, political tension, and philosophical weight of the discussions around the Uniform Civil Code (UCC). When this subject surfaced—primarily during the debates on what was then Draft Article 35 (later Article 44)—it stirred not just legal arguments but anxieties born from centuries of religious practice, community identity, and the fragile atmosphere of a country still recovering from Partition.
The idea of a Uniform Civil Code was not new. Reformers had discussed it since the nineteenth century, and the British had declined to impose uniformity because they feared disturbing religious sensibilities. In 194G–49, however, India was turning into a secular republic. In such a state, was it acceptable for marriage, divorce, inheritance, and adoption to remain governed by separate personal laws for different religious communities? Many Assembly members believed the answer was no. Others felt that pushing uniformity too quickly would fracture a newly bruised nation.
The debate came to life when the Assembly considered placing the UCC among the enforceable fundamental rights. Members like M. R. Masani, Hansa Mehta, and Rajkumari Amrit Kaur were among the strongest advocates of a uniform code. These women, in particular, argued from a perspective forged in struggles for gender equality and social reform. They believed that personal laws had, in many cases, entrenched gender discrimination. For them, equality before the law required one secular civil code for all Indians, regardless of religion. Their positions are documented in the
Subcommittee on Fundamental Rights and referenced again during the Assembly’s debates in late 1948.
Source: CLPR (Centre for Law and Policy Research) historical constitutional archives [https://clpr.org.in/wp-content/uploads/2017/11/UCC-Part-1-Constitutional-History.pdf]{.underline}
But the opposition to an immediate uniform code was equally strong. Muslim members of the Assembly feared that abolishing community-specific personal laws at that moment would deepen a sense of vulnerability among people who were still reeling from Partition violence. Religious minorities, not only Muslims, expressed unease at the thought of the state stepping into domains traditionally left to religious authority. Some argued that personal laws were not merely legal matters but expressions of identity, woven into rituals, ceremonies, family customs, and centuries of practice.
When the debate reached the floor, it was Dr. B. R. Ambedkar who found himself at the centre of the storm. As the chairman of the Drafting Committee, he had to decide where the UCC should appear in the Constitution. If it were placed among fundamental rights, it would become enforceable through the courts. If it were placed in the Directive Principles, it would serve as a constitutional aspiration rather than an immediate legal requirement.
Ambedkar’s position was nuanced. He believed in the long-term necessity of a Uniform Civil Code. He argued that while the state should eventually reform the fragmented civil law system, it could not ignore the social realities of 1949. His speeches, preserved in the Assembly’s records and in later compilations, reflect a careful balance. Ambedkar insisted that no community could claim an absolute right to resist social reform. At the same time, he recognized that the state should not impose change without preparing society for it. He proposed placing the UCC in the Directive Principles under the logic that strong constitutional encouragement would enable gradual reform through persuasion rather than coercion.
The compromise was accepted. Draft Article 35 became Article 44, declaring that “The State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India.” Those who feared state interference took comfort in the fact that the provision was non-justiciable. Reformers took comfort in the fact that the Constitution expressed an aspiration for eventual legal unification.
Yet the debate did not end in the chamber. Newspapers across the country covered the arguments intensely. Women’s rights groups saw the outcome as only a partial victory. Conservative voices, on the other hand, interpreted the placement of the UCC in the Directive Principles as evidence that the Assembly understood the need for sensitivity in matters of personal law. The public reaction mirrored the diversity of the Assembly itself.
In hindsight, the UCC debate stands out as one of the earliest tests of India’s model of secularism. The Assembly had to answer a difficult question: Should secularism be defined as strict uniformity of laws or as a delicate coexistence between religious personal laws and the power of the state? The compromise they chose—placing the UCC among the Directive Principles—has shaped legal and political debates for the next seven decades.
Reading the Assembly records today, one can sense the tension in the room. People spoke not only as legislators but as representatives of communities struggling with fear, hope, and memory. The UCC debate, perhaps more than any other, captured the moral complexity of constitution-making in a country that had to reinvent itself while healing from its deepest wounds. It was a reminder that a Constitution is not only a legal document but also a mirror of the social moment from which it emerges.
The Fierce Battle Over Secularism — How the Constituent Assembly Chose a Path Between Faith and State#When the Constituent Assembly confronted the question of secularism, it found itself navigating not only legal theory but centuries of social tension, colonial policy, and the very fresh wounds of Partition. The Assembly had declared early on that India would not be a theocracy. Yet what that meant in practice was far less obvious. Should the state maintain strict separation from religion, as in France? Should it adopt the American model of non-establishment but maximal freedom? Or should it articulate something distinct—an Indian form of secularism that allowed the state to intervene in religion when necessary to ensure reform? These questions echoed across several sessions of the Assembly, and the debates that followed shaped one of the most important features of the Indian Constitution.
The issue did not come to the Assembly in a single, neatly packaged clause. It appeared in multiple places: in the Preamble, in fundamental rights guaranteeing freedom of religion, in provisions regulating untouchability, temple entry, and reform of religious institutions, and in the discussions on the Uniform Civil Code. The complexity of the Indian social fabric meant that secularism was not simply a matter of keeping religion out of the state. Rather, it required the state to navigate caste, gender, religious diversity, and centuries-old customs that blended spiritual and social life.
One of the earliest and strongest voices pressing for an explicit commitment to secularism was K. T. Shah, a tireless member of the Assembly whose interventions were frequent and philosophically sharp.
Shah repeatedly argued that the Constitution should explicitly describe India as a “secular” state, and at one point even suggested the formulation “Secular, Federal, Socialist Union of States.” His proposals appear throughout the Assembly’s records. He believed that unless the Constitution itself used the word “secular,” India might drift toward majoritarian dominance or allow religion to influence governance in ways that threatened liberty. His amendments, however, were consistently rejected.
Source: RGICS (Rajiv Gandhi Institute for Contemporary Studies) archival analysis of Constituent Assembly debates on secularism
[https://www.rgics.org/democracy/secularism-in-the-constituent-assembly-debates-194G-1950/]{.underline}
Shah’s proposals met resistance from many members, including Ambedkar, who felt that secularism was already woven into the fabric of the Constitution through the fundamental rights chapter. Ambedkar believed that constitutional guarantees of religious freedom, combined with the prohibition of untouchability and the state’s power to regulate secular aspects of religious practice, were sufficient to establish a secular state without using the word explicitly. Ambedkar argued that embedding ideological labels directly into the text might constrain future democratic choices or reduce constitutional principles to slogans rather than substantive guarantees.
Others expressed a different concern—that an overly assertive secular state could alienate minorities at a time when Partition had left communities psychologically fragile. Some Muslim members, while committed to a secular India, worried about the state exercising power over religious practices. They felt the Constitution’s role should be to safeguard equality rather than dictate social reform from above. The Assembly had to acknowledge these fears while also recognizing that India could not remain hostage to religious privilege or discriminatory custom.
The debates reached their most delicate point when the Assembly discussed Articles 25 to 28—the provisions guaranteeing freedom of religion. The Assembly had to determine how far religious freedom extended and where social reform began. Ambedkar made one of his most significant interventions here, arguing that the state must retain the authority to regulate the secular aspects of religion. He insisted that essential matters of faith were protected, but practices rooted in social hierarchy or discrimination could not be shielded by invoking religion. Ambedkar’s reasoning is documented clearly in the Assembly’s records: he argued that religion in India often intertwined with economics and social stratification, and the Constitution could not permit oppressive customs to flourish behind the veil of religious autonomy.
Through these debates, a uniquely Indian vision of secularism began to take shape. Rather than a complete withdrawal of the state from religion, Indian secularism became a principle of equal respect for all religions combined with the authority to intervene for social reform and equality. This was
drastically different from the Western models that inspired some members. Indian secularism would neither create a radical separation nor permit religious law to supersede fundamental rights.
The Assembly’s eventual decision not to include the word “secular” explicitly in the Constitution did not reflect indifference. Instead, it reflected a consensus that secularism needed to operate through rights, limitations, and protections rather than through a single declaratory label. The Constitution’s provisions—prohibiting religious discrimination, ensuring equal access to public institutions, abolishing untouchability, and allowing state regulation of secular aspects of religious practice—became the operational architecture of secularism in India.
Decades later, in 197G, the 42nd Amendment inserted the words “socialist” and “secular” into the Preamble. But by then, the principles had already lived in the text for a generation. The framers had chosen substance over slogan. They built a secular state bit by bit, not by proclamation, but by embedding equality, freedom of conscience, dignity, and state responsibility into the basic structure of the Constitution.
Looking back, the secularism debates show the Assembly at its most reflective and cautious. They reveal how deeply the members understood the delicacy of India’s social landscape and how carefully they attempted to balance religious freedom with social justice. The India they envisioned was one where the state neither favoured nor suppressed any religion, but ensured that citizenship—not religious identity—formed the basis of equal rights.
The Battle Over Economic Rights — Why the Assembly Chose Aspirations Over Enforceability#When the Constituent Assembly turned to the question of economic and social rights, the atmosphere shifted from legal drafting to a deeper moral struggle. India had just emerged from colonial exploitation, staggering poverty, sharp social hierarchy, and the trauma of Partition. Many members hoped the Constitution would not only guarantee political freedoms but also promise security, livelihood, education, and dignity to the poorest citizens. They believed that liberty alone was not meaningful without the material conditions that allowed people to live with fairness and self-respect.
This desire for broad social justice led several members to argue that economic rights—such as the right to work, the right to a living wage, the right to education, and the right to social security—should be incorporated directly into the chapter on Fundamental Rights. If these rights were fundamental, they
would be enforceable in the courts, and the state would be obligated to guarantee them without delay. Voices like K. T. Shah, Hansa Mehta, and others pressed for such guarantees in different ways. They insisted that freedom from hunger and access to basic welfare were as essential to democracy as protection against censorship or unlawful detention.
But there was another perspective, articulated most prominently by Dr. B. R. Ambedkar during the debate on November 19, 1948. Ambedkar agreed wholeheartedly that the state had an obligation to pursue social and economic transformation. Yet he warned that making these rights immediately enforceable would create an impossible burden. The Assembly had to acknowledge that the state, at that moment, did not possess the financial, administrative, or institutional capacity to guarantee employment, education, housing, and other welfare rights to every citizen. If these rights were declared fundamental but the government failed to fulfil them—which was a certainty—the Constitution would lose credibility from the outset.
