Even well-intentioned governments, he said, were tempted to hide waste, bypass procedure, or ignore financial discipline unless someone uncompromising stood watch.
His speech, though calm, was laced with urgency. India was about to embark on massive public spending — dams, roads, industries, agricultural reforms. Without a fiercely independent auditor, the dream of development could collapse into corruption or mismanagement.
Then Ananthasayanam Ayyangar, one of the Assembly’s most thoughtful members, rose to speak. His tone was gentle, but his words hit hard. He said that of all the officers the Constitution would create, the Auditor General must be the one who could “sit in judgment over the government itself.” He reminded his colleagues that they were writing a Constitution not just for heroes and idealists but for future governments too — governments that might be careless, incompetent, or even corrupt. The Constitution, he said, must protect the country from the worst possibilities, not simply hope for the best.
But the real turning point came when B. R. Ambedkar took the floor.
Ambedkar had fought for strong institutions throughout the constitution-making process, but on this subject, he spoke with unusual firmness. The Auditor General, he said, had to be as independent as the Supreme Court. He must not serve at the pleasure of the executive. He must not report to the Cabinet. He must not be influenced by ministers or bureaucrats. His only master must be the Constitution itself.
Ambedkar explained that the British system, though colonial and oppressive, had one admirable institution — the Auditor General’s independence. It had acted as a check on the colonial administration’s spending. If the British permitted that much accountability in a regime that did not answer to Indians, how could free India accept anything less?
As he spoke, the Assembly listened with rare stillness. Ambedkar laid out the vision of an Auditor General who would be fearless, untouchable by political pressure, and answerable only to Parliament. His language grew sharper as he described the dangers of executive interference. If the Auditor General were made subordinate to the government, he said, “all our financial safeguards will be but a rope of sand.”
Those words landed heavily. A rope of sand — a Constitution powerless to enforce discipline, a republic vulnerable to waste and misuse.
What followed surprised even seasoned observers of the Assembly. Not a single member opposed Ambedkar’s vision. Even those who had been skeptical moments earlier seemed moved by the clarity of the argument. One after another, members from different regions and political backgrounds voiced
their agreement. They wanted the Auditor General to be uncompromising. They wanted a guardian who would stand above politics.
The Assembly went even further. It adopted provisions giving the CAG security of tenure, protection from arbitrary removal, complete control over staff, and independence in reporting. The CAG would not only audit the Union and the states; he would be insulated from the very authorities he was auditing. It was a remarkable act of constitutional courage.
When the final clause was read aloud, the mood shifted from intensity to quiet satisfaction. The Assembly knew it had created something precious — an institution that would outlive governments, outlast political parties, and watch over the nation’s treasury long after the framers themselves were gone.
In later decades, it would be the CAG who exposed scandals, questioned expenditures, and held power to account when few others dared. But all of that was still in the future.
In that moment, on 30 May 1949, the framers made a choice that revealed their deepest instincts: that the republic must protect itself not only through lofty ideals but through vigilant, unglamorous, relentless oversight. They had seen enough of how power could corrupt. So they created a sentinel who would be fearless even in the face of the government.
The CAG was not born with applause or drama. He was born through a quiet act of principled conviction.
And in that quietness lies the strength of one of India’s most remarkable constitutional institutions.
The Safeguards Debate — When Ambedkar Defended a Clause He Admitted He “Disliked’'#There were days in the Constituent Assembly when the air felt heavy with principle, and then there were days when it felt heavy with sorrow. The debate on preventive detention safeguards on 15 September 1949 was one of the latter. It came after the Assembly had already accepted the painful reality that preventive detention — the power to imprison a person without trial — would find a place in the Constitution. But accepting the principle was only half the battle. The Assembly now had to write the safeguards: the minimum protections that would stop this extraordinary power from becoming a tool of tyranny.
That morning, the hall opened with an uncomfortable stillness. Many members had spent the previous evening agonising over the draft. In their hearts, they knew preventive detention contradicted the spirit of the Constitution they were trying to build. They had lived under a colonial government that used it without compassion. They had seen their friends, their colleagues, their leaders jailed with no trial, no explanation, no remedy. And now they were being asked to craft the same instrument into the law of a free nation.
The first voice to break the silence was H. V. Kamath, who spoke with an almost moral tremor in his voice. He said preventive detention was a “relic of despotism,” something that should never stain the Constitution of a democracy. He reminded the Assembly that the British had used this power to crush the freedom movement, to silence dissent, to control the people. Would a free India now use the same weapon? Would the victims of yesterday become the wielders of the same tool tomorrow?
Kamath’s speech touched something raw. For a moment, the Assembly seemed united in discomfort.
Then K. M. Munshi rose in defence of the clause, but even he did so with visible reluctance. He did not pretend the provision was noble. He spoke instead of the chaotic world outside the Assembly: the scars of Partition, the floods of refugees, the communal flare-ups, the fear that violence could erupt unpredictably in a country still stitching itself together. A Constitution, he argued, must protect liberty — but it must also protect life. How could the State defend its people without tools to prevent violence before it happened?
The argument did not comfort everyone. Some members shifted uneasily. Others stared at the papers in front of them, unwilling to meet the eyes of their colleagues. Everyone understood both sides too well.
It was then that B. R. Ambedkar rose. He walked slowly, with a heaviness that the House had only seen a few times before — once during the drafting of the reservation clause, and again during the minority rights debate. When he reached the podium, he paused. His voice, when it emerged, was steady but subdued.
He began by saying something that startled even those who knew him best: “I personally dislike this article.” It was rare for Ambedkar to confess personal misgivings in the middle of a constitutional defence. But this time, he did. He said he knew the dangers. He knew the abuses. He knew how fragile liberty was. And yet, he said, the Drafting Committee could not pretend India lived in a world of perfect peace. The country was still recovering from the wounds of Partition. It had seen armed uprisings, assassinations, communal tension, and border insecurity. Under such conditions, the State needed the power to act swiftly.
He spoke of preventive detention as a “necessary evil,” a phrase that hung in the air like smoke. It captured perfectly the tension between idealism and survival. No one in the Assembly wanted it. But no one could deny the reality outside the Assembly doors.
What Ambedkar fought for that day was not the principle of preventive detention, but the safeguards. He insisted that the State must be constitutionally required to explain the grounds of arrest “as soon as may be,” that detainees must have the right to representation, that an independent advisory board must review every case, that prison terms must be strictly limited. If the Constitution must allow this dangerous power, he said, it must also cage it.
Several members softened after his speech. Even those who hated the clause admitted that Ambedkar had done everything possible to protect liberty within the constraints of a wounded nation.
When the vote was finally taken, the House passed the clause with the safeguards. There was no applause. There never is when a constitutional decision feels like a compromise with tragedy. Members returned to their seats quietly, some pensive, some resigned. They had not written a perfect article. They had written a necessary one.
Years later, preventive detention would be invoked in ways the framers feared. It would be abused, stretched, misused during the Emergency, and criticised by courts and scholars alike. But none of that was visible on the September afternoon when Ambedkar stood in the Assembly and admitted he disliked the very clause he was defending. All that was visible in that moment was honesty, sorrow, and the heavy responsibility of constitution-making in a broken time.
It was one of those rare moments when the Assembly did not feel triumphant or visionary. It felt human — painfully human.
The Scheduled Areas Debate — When Jaipal Singh Munda Reminded the Assembly That Adivasis Had Never Been Conquered#On 5 September 1949, the Constituent Assembly turned to a subject that many members knew was important but few fully understood: the administration of Scheduled Areas and the protection of Adivasi communities. The hall that morning felt different. The usual confidence, the usual tug-of-war between competing ideologies, gave way to something else — uncertainty. Many in the room were lawyers, academics, freedom fighters, but only a handful truly knew the world they were about to
legislate for: the vast forested regions where millions of India’s tribal peoples lived, governed by their own customs, their own systems of justice, their own sense of dignity.
And sitting among them was Jaipal Singh Munda, the man who understood that world better than any of them.
When Jaipal Singh entered the Assembly, he carried with him not just the authority of being an Oxford-educated intellectual, a former Indian Civil Service probationer, and the captain of India’s first Olympic hockey team. He carried the unbroken lineage of the Munda people of Chhotanagpur — a community that had resisted wave after wave of external domination. He often said proudly that Adivasis were “the original inhabitants of India,” and he meant it literally. His speeches were different from those of the other members. They came not from books or legal texts, but from lived history.
As the debate began, Sardar Patel’s advisory committee report was placed before the Assembly. It recommended special protections for tribal areas: restricted land transfers, limits on outside encroachment, and the establishment of autonomous councils in the Northeast. Patel, who had spent months grappling with the incredible diversity and political fragility of the tribal belts, believed these provisions were essential to prevent exploitation by moneylenders, contractors, landlords, and even overzealous administrators.
But the Assembly was unsure. Some members feared that giving tribals separate protections might create isolation or “separatism.” Others felt the Constitution must integrate all citizens uniformly. A few questioned whether Adivasis were prepared for self-governance in the modern constitutional sense. The tone of the debate began drifting into paternalism — the kind of well-meaning condescension that had always followed Adivasis through history.
Then Jaipal Singh stood up.
The moment he rose, the mood changed. Members who normally shuffled papers or leaned back during speeches straightened in their seats. Everyone knew something important was about to be said.
Jaipal Singh began quietly, but with unmistakable authority. He reminded the Assembly that the Adivasi world was older than any kingdom represented in the hall. His people, he said, had lived in India long before any of the Aryan, Dravidian, or Mughal polities existed. They had governed themselves through their own institutions — village councils, community assemblies, customary law
— with a dignity that came not from state recognition but from tradition and memory.
Then he said the sentence that became one of the most extraordinary moments in the Constituent Assembly’s history:
“We have never been conquered. The British were the first to come into contact with us.”
The hall fell silent. The words cut through the paternalism instantly. Adivasis were not backward subjects to be uplifted by charity; they were free people whose autonomy had been interrupted only by colonial power. Jaipal Singh was not speaking from theory. He was speaking from a cultural memory of independence that stretched centuries before the British arrived.
He went further. He said the Adivasi relationship with the Indian state had always been one of distance, sometimes suspicion, often indifference. If the new Constitution wanted Adivasis to trust this republic, it had to treat them not as wards of the state but as equal partners in the national project
partners whose unique ways of life deserved respect, not assimilation. What made his speech unforgettable was the pain woven into its pride. He spoke of the exploitation the Adivasis had suffered — the land grabbers, the forest officers who treated them like trespassers in their own home, the moneylenders who trapped them in debt, the administrators who dismissed their customs as primitive. He said the tribal people of India had been loyal to the land, to the forests, to their traditions — but the land had not been loyal to them.
The Assembly absorbed his words with a kind of quiet shame.
For a brief moment, the great lawyers and statesmen of the Assembly — men who had debated the highest principles of liberty and equality — realised that the Adivasis had never asked for lofty theories. They had asked only for protection from exploitation and the freedom to live by their own customs.
By the end of his speech, it was clear to everyone that the Constitution had to include special protections. Not because Adivasis were weak, but because they had been made vulnerable by a history that was not of their making.
When the final provisions were adopted — what would later become the Fifth and Sixth Schedules — the Assembly felt a rare sense of moral responsibility fulfilled. These schedules guaranteed autonomy in the Northeast, protection of tribal land, and governance structures sensitive to local customs. They were not perfect. They would be challenged, diluted, and contested in later decades. But they were a beginning — a constitutional acknowledgment of the dignity and distinctiveness of India’s first peoples.
As Jaipal Singh sat down, many members looked moved, even humbled. They had been reminded that the Constitution was not merely a legal text. It was a pact with all of India — including those whose voices had too often been ignored.
On that September afternoon, the Assembly did something more profound than pass a constitutional clause. It listened. And in listening, it honoured a history older than the republic itself.
The Presidential Debate — When the Assembly Swore India Would Never Have Another Emperor#On 14 December 1948, the Constituent Assembly turned to the question that would define the character of the Indian republic: What kind of President should India have? A ceremonial head of state? A powerful executive? Something in between? The debate was not only constitutional — it was emotional, almost visceral. Many in the room had spent their entire lives resisting a system in which one figure, the Viceroy, held unimaginable authority over millions. They had marched against imperial proclamations, been jailed for opposing arbitrary decrees, and watched decisions affecting their lives made in distant rooms by a single, unelected man.
No one in the Assembly wanted to write a Constitution that risked creating another such figure.
The debate began with an unease that permeated the room. The Draft Constitution proposed a President who was elected, not hereditary; constitutional, not autocratic; bound by the advice of ministers, not independent of them. Yet, the memories of British rule ran deep, and the Assembly was unwilling to accept any trace of centralized personal authority.
The first voice that carried the room was K. T. Shah, a brilliant but often contrarian figure whose interventions always forced the Assembly to think harder. Shah argued that the President must be directly elected by the people. Anything less, he said, would dilute the democratic character of the republic. If the President was to represent the nation, he must receive his mandate from the public itself, not from an electoral college.
His speech stirred several members, but it also sparked anxiety. Direct elections would give the President an independent democratic legitimacy — a mandate parallel to that of the Prime Minister. Members feared that this could create two rival centres of power, leading to instability or even a constitutional crisis.
Into this tension stepped Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, who rose with the calm assurance of a man who had spent a lifetime studying constitutional systems. His voice was gentle, but it carried enormous intellectual weight. A directly elected President, he warned, could claim to speak for the people in ways that might challenge the authority of Parliament. India could not afford a divided executive. The President must represent the unity of the state, not the dynamism of electoral politics.
His words landed with an almost physical impact. The Assembly had seen firsthand how dangerous concentrated authority could be. Federal unity in 1949 was still fragile. A too-powerful President could undo what they had painstakingly built.
Then, as the tension crested, Jawaharlal Nehru rose.
Nehru did not speak like a lawyer or a theoretician. He spoke like a man who had seen the worst of absolute power and did not want his country to repeat the mistake. He said that India must not create offices that encouraged ambition. “We do not want strong men,” he said in a quiet but firm voice. “We want strong institutions.” A directly elected President might become a figure around whom authoritarian tendencies could gather. India, he argued, needed stability, not personality.
The Assembly fell silent. There was something deeply honest about Nehru’s tone — an understanding that India’s political culture was still raw, that a grand, charismatic head of state could easily overshadow Parliament, the Cabinet, and the Prime Minister.
And then came B. R. Ambedkar.
Ambedkar rose with the calm resolve of a man who knew exactly how to strike the balance India needed. He explained that the President was being designed as a constitutional figure — someone who symbolised the nation but did not govern it. Real executive power would rest with the Council of Ministers, headed by the Prime Minister. To give the President a direct popular mandate would threaten the very parliamentary structure the Assembly had agreed upon.
Ambedkar added something even more striking. The Indian President, unlike the American one, would have no independent authority to act against the wishes of the Cabinet. A direct election, therefore, would mislead the public into thinking the President held a power he in fact did not possess. The Constitution must not create illusions, he said; it must reflect the truth of how power would actually be exercised.
What made Ambedkar’s speech so compelling was that he wasn’t merely rejecting Shah’s proposal — he was teaching the Assembly how to think about power: not as a symbol or a title, but as a structure that must be carefully balanced to avoid tyranny.
As the discussion deepened, fears of the colonial past resurfaced. Members remembered how the Viceroy had overturned elected governments, dismissed ministries, and acted with imperial arrogance. Anything that resembled that office — even faintly — was unacceptable.
By the time the debate concluded, the Assembly had formed a clear consensus. India’s President would be elected by an electoral college to ensure legitimacy, but not by the public directly. He would be respected but not powerful, dignified but not decisive, a guardian of the Constitution but not its wielder.
When the clause was adopted, the mood was one of quiet relief. The Assembly had taken a stand against concentrated personal power, against the possibility of a future dictator emerging under the guise of a presidential mandate. They had chosen a modest presidency — not because they lacked imagination, but because they understood history too well.
In that moment, India was making a promise to itself:
Never again would one person stand above the people.
Never again would personal authority overshadow democratic institutions. Never again would India submit to an emperor — whether foreign or domestic.
And that promise, forged in the quiet dignity of the Constituent Assembly, became one of the defining features of the Indian republic.
The Impeachment Debate — When the Assembly Protected the Republic From Its Own President#The question before the Constituent Assembly on 29 December 1948 was as delicate as it was profound: How should India remove its President if he violates the Constitution? It was a question that touched the deepest anxieties of any democracy. What happens when the highest constitutional officer
the very symbol of national unity — betrays the office entrusted to him? The hall that winter afternoon was quiet in a way that signalled seriousness rather than fatigue. This was not a debate about policy or administration. It was about safeguarding the republic from the possibility — however remote — that the President might misuse the dignity of his office.
The debate opened with Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, the Assembly’s constitutional philosopher, explaining why impeachment must be possible but difficult. He said the President must not fear removal for political reasons, but he must remain accountable for grave constitutional violations. His voice was calm, but he acknowledged the emotional weight of the task. “We are dealing,” he said, “with an office that must be honoured, yet controlled.” It was the tension at the heart of the debate.
But what stirred the Assembly most was not the legal intricacy. It was the memory of India’s own difficult relationship with executive power. Only a few years earlier, the Viceroy had overturned elected governments with a single signature. Members remembered too clearly how concentrated authority could crush self-rule. They were determined that such power must never again go unchecked — not even in the hands of a President chosen by the nation.
As the discussion progressed, a surprising voice entered the floor: Prof. Shibban Lal Saksena, known for his fierce independence and his habit of questioning every assumption. He warned the Assembly that making impeachment too difficult would place the President beyond accountability. What if a corrupt or authoritarian President simply refused to resign? What if he interfered with elections or misused his constitutional discretion? Saksena spoke with the urgency of a man who had watched democracy suppressed under colonial rule. “We must not,” he said, “create another throne.”
His warning left the hall uneasy.
Soon after, H. V. Kamath rose with equal passion. He argued that impeachment should be rare, but not impossible. He reminded the Assembly of the American example, where impeachment existed not as a political weapon but as a constitutional safeguard. The public must know, he said, that even the President is not above the Constitution.
But the decision — and the tone of the debate — ultimately rested on the shoulders of B. R. Ambedkar.
When Ambedkar stood up, the hall quieted. He began by acknowledging a simple truth: impeachment is an extreme remedy. It must not be used to punish presidents for unpopular decisions or political disagreements. It must be reserved for something far more serious — a “violation of the Constitution.” He stressed that the President was not the head of government, and therefore had limited personal
authority. His powers were largely ceremonial, exercised on the advice of the Prime Minister. Because of this, Ambedkar argued, impeachment should be rare.
But then he added something that settled the debate.
He said the Constitution must contain a clear, solemn, and public method of removing the President because no office, however dignified, could be beyond constitutional control. “The President,” Ambedkar said, “is as much subject to the Constitution as any other citizen of India.” And if breaching the Constitution carried no consequence, then the entire document would be a hollow promise.
The Assembly listened with a mixture of respect and resolve. There was something reassuring in Ambedkar’s willingness to confront the uncomfortable. He did not pretend that the President would never go wrong. He created a system strong enough to survive even if he did.
The final method adopted — requiring a two-thirds majority of Parliament after a formal charge and a full investigation — reflected the Assembly’s balancing act. Removal had to be possible, but only after overwhelming evidence and overwhelming consensus. It had to be difficult enough to protect the President from political attacks, yet clear enough to protect the country from presidential misconduct.
When the clause was passed, the silence that followed felt almost ceremonial. Members understood they had just created one of the republic’s most solemn tools — a mechanism that would hopefully never be used, but must exist in case the protector of the Constitution ever threatened it.
What makes this episode extraordinary is the maturity the Assembly displayed. No one spoke of political advantage. No one tried to weaken the presidency out of fear or strengthen it out of reverence. They wrote the impeachment clause with humility — the humility of a young nation determined to safeguard its future, even from the possibility of its own leaders.
And perhaps that is the heart of the anecdote: the framers trusted democracy enough to give it a remedy against its own highest officer, yet trusted the presidency enough to make that remedy hard to invoke. It was a balance only a wise Assembly could strike.
On that December afternoon in 1948, the Constituent Assembly made a quiet promise to the nation: No one — not even the President — would stand above the Constitution.
The Finance Commission Debate — When the Assembly Insisted the Union Must Never Treat the States Like Dependents#On 9 August 1949, the Constituent Assembly gathered to debate something that, on its surface, looked like a technical matter: the creation of a Finance Commission. But the moment the discussion began, it became clear that this was no dry administrative clause. Beneath the legal language lay a question that could decide the fate of Indian federalism: How would the young Union share financial power with its states?
The hall that morning felt unusually thoughtful. India’s federal structure was still being shaped, and financial autonomy was its nervous system. Without money, no state could run schools, build roads, maintain police forces, or carry out welfare programmes. A Constitution could declare states free, but if the purse strings rested entirely with the Union, that “freedom” would be illusory. The Assembly understood that they were shaping not only fiscal machinery, but the balance of power in the Union itself.
The first voice to animate the room was K. Santhanam, a thoughtful member with a deep understanding of administrative realities. He warned that financial centralisation was as dangerous as political centralisation. If New Delhi controlled too much revenue, states would become beggars before the Centre, forced to lobby for funds instead of governing confidently. His tone was firm but calm, and it resonated across the hall. India needed unity, but not dependency. Cooperation, but not fiscal domination.
Then came H. V. Kamath, who sharpened the argument further. He said the Constitution should never allow the Centre to treat states like “subordinates.” A strong Centre was necessary, yes — the trauma of Partition had taught that lesson well — but a Centre so strong that it could starve a state financially would weaken the entire federal fabric. Kamath’s words carried the unmistakable echo of someone who had watched colonial administrators treat India’s provinces as weak dependents. Free India could not replicate that pattern, even unintentionally.
But the debate took a deeper turn when T. T. Krishnamachari rose to speak. He brought to the table not only logic but a quiet emotional force. He reminded the Assembly of how different India’s provinces were — economically, socially, geographically. Some were rich in agricultural output. Some had mineral wealth. Some were poor and still reeling from the administrative upheaval caused by Partition or princely state integration. If the Constitution did not create an impartial mechanism for determining how revenue should be shared, these inequalities would deepen.
He warned that states must not be reduced to pleading for grants based on political favour or regional bargaining. The country needed an institution that could stand above politics and decide with fairness, objectivity, and dignity.
This argument set the stage for one of the most important interventions of the day — that of B. R. Ambedkar.
Ambedkar had designed the Draft Constitution’s financial provisions with almost surgical precision. When he rose, the Assembly sensed that something essential was about to be explained. He began by acknowledging a reality no one could deny: India was a federation in name, but it was entering independence with deep economic imbalances and administrative strains. The Centre needed resources to rebuild the nation. But so did the states. Neither could afford to dominate the other.
Ambedkar’s voice was steady as he laid out the purpose of the Finance Commission. It would be an independent constitutional body — not a department under the executive, not a parliamentary committee, not an advisory group vulnerable to political shifts — but a permanent, impartial institution to recommend how revenue should be distributed between the Union and the states.
He explained that the framers wanted to avoid what had happened in many other federations around the world, where financial disputes had paralysed cooperation. The Finance Commission was the solution: a buffer, a judge, a reconciler, and a guarantor that the principles of federal fairness would survive beyond the goodwill of any political party or leader.
As Ambedkar spoke, the Assembly realised the deeper significance of what was being created. They were not designing a fiscal body; they were writing a guarantee of trust. A guarantee that the Union would not hoard revenue. A guarantee that every state — big or small, rich or poor — would have a constitutional claim to financial dignity.
There was something profoundly moral in Ambedkar’s explanation. He said the Commission must be insulated from political pressure because fiscal justice was too important to be left to political moods. The Constitution must protect states not only from overreach but from financial starvation.
By the time he finished, the hall had grown still. Even members who had been uncertain or sceptical earlier appeared moved by the clarity of his vision.
The debate continued, but the direction was set. Members understood they were enshrining not a bureaucratic device but a vital pillar of cooperative federalism. When the clause was finally adopted, there was a sense of quiet achievement. The Assembly knew that India was entering independence as a
fragile federation, with states of very different sizes, resources, and histories. A lesser Constitution might have ignored that reality. The framers chose instead to confront it with wisdom.
Years later, the Finance Commission would become one of India’s most respected institutions, shaping the country’s fiscal landscape across generations. But all of that began on that August day in 1949, when the Assembly insisted that the Union must never treat its states as dependents, and states must never fear the Centre.
What makes Anecdote 44 remarkable is not the technicality of the financial provisions. It is the instinct that guided them — an instinct rooted in fairness, humility, and a deep understanding that the strength of a union lies not in the power of the Centre, but in the dignity of its parts.
On that day, the Assembly made a promise that India still leans on: A federation must be built not on power, but on trust.
The Public Service Commission Debate — When the Assembly Shielded Bureaucrats From Political Winds#On 19 August 1949, the Constituent Assembly turned to an issue that rarely provokes excitement among the public but is vital to the health of any democracy: the independence of the Public Service Commissions. It was a day that revealed the Assembly’s deepest understanding of how fragile administrations can be, and how easily a government can crumble if its civil servants are not protected from political pressure.
The atmosphere that day was thoughtful rather than tense. The members knew they were not debating something dramatic like fundamental rights or the powers of the President. But they also knew that without an honest, impartial, competent bureaucracy, every other constitutional promise could collapse. They had lived through years of arbitrary colonial administration, and they knew how essential it was to design a system where appointments, promotions, and discipline were insulated from political manipulation.
The first major voice belonged to Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, whose calm reasoning always carried weight. He rose to explain why a Public Service Commission could not simply be a department under the executive. If the future of the civil service was placed directly under ministers, he warned, corruption would rise, favouritism would flourish, and the administration would become an instrument of political reward. Alladi’s tone was not dramatic; it was sober, grounded in experience.
He reminded the Assembly that a democracy could not afford a civil service afraid to speak truth to power.
After Alladi sat down, T. T. Krishnamachari stepped in with even stronger language. He declared bluntly that the colonial bureaucracy had been autocratic, yes — but also remarkably insulated from political pressure. Free India’s bureaucracy must be different in spirit, more humane and people-oriented, but it must retain the same independence. He said that if the Constitution allowed ministers to meddle freely in appointments or transfers, the entire administrative fabric would unravel. Civil servants would become tools of the ruling party, not servants of the nation.
There was something honest and almost vulnerable in his argument. India, he said, was entering a phase of intense political excitement. Political parties were forming, breaking, and reforming. In such a climate, unless the civil service remained neutral and secure, it would not survive its first decade.
But perhaps the most striking intervention came from H. V. Kamath, who always carried his idealism into the chamber like a torch. Kamath argued passionately that public servants must be protected not only from political pressure but from the temptation of political patronage. His voice rose as he said that civil servants should not feel obliged to any politician for their jobs or promotions. They must feel beholden only to the Constitution and the people. If India allowed political interference to become the culture of administration, he warned, “the rot will set in from the top.”
These arguments set the stage for the voice everyone had been waiting for — B. R. Ambedkar.
When Ambedkar rose, the room grew quiet. He was not just defending the Draft Constitution; he was fighting for a principle he believed essential for the republic’s survival. His voice was measured, but the force of his reasoning was unmistakable.
He said that Public Service Commissions must be independent constitutional bodies, not creatures of the executive. Their members must have security of tenure, protection from arbitrary removal, and financial independence. He explained that the experience of the British era had taught one clear lesson: when political influence enters the machinery of appointments, the entire administration corrodes.
Then Ambedkar said something that has echoed through decades of constitutional interpretation: the civil service is the “invisible machinery” that keeps the state running even when political tempests rage. Ministers will come and go. Governments will rise and fall. But the administration must endure. And it can endure only if it is protected from political interference.
The Assembly absorbed these words with seriousness. Many members were future ministers themselves. They knew how tempting it could be for future governments — not just the opposition — to control appointments and promotions. Yet they also recognised that the Constitution must rise above personal temptation.
As the debates continued, the Assembly reached a rare consensus. The Public Service Commissions must be constitutionally entrenched. Their independence must be protected. Their functions — examinations, recruitment, disciplinary advice — must be beyond the reach of political bargaining.
By the end of the day, the Assembly had forged an institution that would become one of India’s strongest administrative pillars. They ensured that civil servants would not live in fear of political reprisal and that talented individuals across the country could enter the administration through open merit, not political connections.
When the clause was adopted, the hall felt quietly proud. There were no dramatic speeches left to give, no ideological battles to fight. What remained was the satisfaction of having built a part of the Constitution that would stand as a shield — not for politicians, not for parties, but for the integrity of governance itself.
Years later, the Public Service Commissions would face criticism, reform, and scrutiny, but the constitutional foundation laid on that August day remained firm. The Assembly’s instinct had been correct: a democracy does not survive on elections alone. It survives on honest administration.
And on 19 August 1949, the Constituent Assembly ensured that India would inherit exactly that — not by chance, but by choice.
The Supreme Court Debate — When the Assembly Decided the Court Must Be Strong Enough to Confront Parliament Itself#The Constituent Assembly had already debated the executive, the legislature, and the civil service by the time it turned, on 24 May 1949, to the question of the Supreme Court of India. But nothing prepared the House for the depth of conviction and emotion that rose when the members began discussing the Court’s powers. It was not a dry legal argument. It was a reckoning with the trauma of colonial rule — years in which courts had often served power rather than justice — and an act of faith in a future where the judiciary would stand tall even against the government.
The morning began with an unusual quiet. Members sat straighter, their faces more attentive. Everyone sensed they were crafting the most important guardian of the Constitution. They were not building an ordinary court. They were building the institution that would, one day, be responsible for telling governments when they had gone too far.
The first major voice that morning belonged to Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, the Assembly’s quiet jurist whose legal wisdom rarely failed to command the room. When Alladi rose, he did not speak like a man presenting a technical clause. He spoke like a man defending a principle that lay at the heart of democracy. He reminded the House that courts were not created merely to settle disputes but to ensure that the government itself remained within constitutional bounds. “A Constitution,” he said, “is not worth the paper it is written on if it does not provide a remedy against its own violation.”
His words carried a weight beyond their volume. Members knew exactly what he meant. They had lived through decades in which law was an instrument of empire, not justice — the Rowlatt Act, the sedition trials, the arrests without trial. A Constitution without a strong court would mean returning to that world, wrapped now in the illusion of freedom.
But the debate took on deeper intensity when M. Ananthasayanam Ayyangar spoke. He talked about the fragility of rights, especially in a country still recovering from Partition violence, mass migrations, and political instability. Legislatures, he warned, are not always calm guardians of liberty. In moments of fear or excitement, even democratic assemblies could pass laws that violated fundamental rights. Someone had to stand above that tide. That someone, he said, must be the Supreme Court.
The room absorbed his words with grave attention. Members understood that they were not only writing for their own time. They were writing for a future they could not yet imagine — for governments they would never meet, for crises they could not foresee, for citizens not yet born.
After several interventions, the eyes of the Assembly turned toward B. R. Ambedkar. When he rose, the hall grew quiet in that familiar way — the silence that meant something foundational was about to be said.
Ambedkar began calmly, almost softly, but the conviction beneath his words was unmistakable. He said that the Supreme Court must be “the sentinel on the qui vive” — the watchman always alert, always awake, always ready to restrain power when it strayed from the Constitution. He spoke not as a theoretician but as someone who understood what unchecked power could do. He had seen oppression not in books but in daily life. He knew how fragile rights were for millions of Indians.
Then he turned to the most crucial point: the Court must have the power to strike down laws passed even by Parliament if those laws violated the Constitution. It was an extraordinary idea in a newborn democracy. Many nations feared giving courts this power, believing it made judges stronger than elected representatives. But Ambedkar insisted that the Constitution, not Parliament, must always be supreme. If the legislature became the final interpreter of its own powers, he said, constitutional limits would collapse.
What he said next became one of the defining statements of the entire Constitution-making process: “In our democracy, the Constitution is supreme. Parliament is not supreme.” The Court, he explained, was the institution that would enforce this supremacy.
The Assembly listened as if absorbing a lesson they knew would outlive them. Ambedkar’s reasoning was simple but profound. The legislature represents the will of the majority, but the Constitution protects the rights of all — especially the minority. When the two collide, someone must arbitrate. That someone must be the judiciary.
The debate continued into the afternoon, but the direction had been set. Members rose one after another to agree that a strong judiciary was not a threat to democracy — it was its backbone. They spoke of the need for judges with independence, dignity, security of tenure, and insulation from political influence. They wanted a Court that could review executive action, protect individual rights, and strike down unconstitutional laws without fear of retribution.
By the time the clause was adopted, the House felt a quiet sense of achievement. They had created an institution that would stand long after they were gone — an institution powerful enough to confront any government in the future.
In later decades, the Supreme Court would strike down constitutional amendments, restrain prime ministers, protect free speech, expand fundamental rights, and sometimes falter. But its authority — the authority to review and invalidate laws — was born on that day in May 1949.
What makes this moment extraordinary is the humility with which the Assembly wrote judicial supremacy into the Constitution. They were elected representatives creating an institution strong enough to limit their own power. It was an act of constitutional self-restraint, rooted in the belief that liberty needed guardians even in a democracy.
On 24 May 1949, the Assembly made a decision that shaped India more than any other: it chose a judiciary strong enough to stand up even to Parliament. A court powerful enough to defend the Constitution, even when the government of the day might want otherwise.
In that moment, the framers entrusted the future of Indian democracy not to men, but to principles
and to the Court that would protect them. The Directive Principles Debate — When the Assembly Called Them the “Conscience of the Constitution”#When the Constituent Assembly turned to the Directive Principles of State Policy on 19 November 1948, many expected a technical discussion about non-justiciable rights. Instead, what unfolded was one of the most emotionally charged, morally resonant debates of the entire constitution-making process — a debate in which members wrestled openly with their dreams for India, their disappointments, and their hopes for generations still unborn.
The hall that morning felt reflective, almost heavy. Members had spent months crafting the enforceable Fundamental Rights, binding the State with obligations it could not ignore. Now they approached provisions that would not be enforceable in courts at all. These were instructions, aspirations, promises
but not rights that a citizen could walk into a court and demand. And that distinction troubled many. The first major voice came from K. T. Shah, who spoke with the intensity of a man who believed deeply in social justice. He argued that it was not enough to write noble goals. If the State was not legally bound to fulfil them, they would become “pious declarations,” nothing more than poetry in the middle of a constitutional text. Shah’s voice sharpened as he said that the poor could not live on promises. They needed enforceable rights — to employment, to education, to fair wages, to social security. Anything short of legal guarantees, he warned, would betray the nation’s moral responsibility.
For a moment, the Assembly fell silent. Shah had touched a nerve.
Then H. V. Kamath rose. He carried neither Shah’s harshness nor his absolutism, but he shared his frustration. He reminded the Assembly that India’s villages were ravaged by poverty, its workers underpaid, its children undernourished. If the Directive Principles remained merely “guiding lights,” what guarantee was there that future governments would not ignore them? His tone was almost pleading — a reminder that ideals, without enforcement, could become illusions.
The debate could have taken a negative turn, descending into cynicism. But then something remarkable happened.
Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, usually so restrained and legalistic, spoke with unusual emotion. He argued that the Directive Principles were not decorative. They were the heart behind the enforceable rights — the moral compass that would orient the Republic for decades. Courts could enforce rights, he said, but principles shaped governance. These directives would stand as “fundamental in the governance of the country.” They were binding — not legally, but morally and politically.
His tone was firm, almost fatherly. He said that making the Directive Principles enforceable was impossible given India’s limited resources. The Constitution could not require the impossible. But it could demand that future governments never forget what they owed to the poor.
Then came the voice everyone waited for — B. R. Ambedkar.
Ambedkar rose slowly, and the room quieted. His relationship to the Directive Principles was complicated. He had fought relentlessly for enforceable rights — especially social and economic ones. He had written passionately about the emptiness of political equality without social and economic equality. Yet he had also witnessed the realities of administrative chaos, financial hardship, and social division in independent India’s first years.
And so he spoke that day with a mixture of realism and hope.
He said the Directive Principles represented the ideal of economic democracy, complementing the political democracy created by Fundamental Rights. They were not enforceable because India did not yet have the resources to make them enforceable. But they were not optional either. He called them “instruments of instruction,” binding future governments morally and politically.
Then he said something that changed the tone of the entire debate: the Directive Principles were “novel to our Constitution” — an audacious attempt to raise the living standards of the nation, not through coercion but through conscience.
Ambedkar’s voice grew more powerful as he insisted that no government could ignore these principles and still claim to be constitutional. They were, he said, “obligations,” not suggestions.
The effect was immediate. The mood shifted from skepticism to understanding. Members realised that the Directive Principles were not weak. They were visionary. They were the blueprint for a future India still waiting to be built.
The most moving intervention came from A. V. Thakkar, known for his work with adivasi and marginalised communities. His voice cracked slightly as he said that the Directive Principles were “the
soul of the Constitution” — the promise that the poor had not been forgotten in the nation’s founding moment. India could not give them everything at once, but it could give them a future.
By the time the debate closed, the Assembly understood the meaning of what they had created. The Directive Principles were not enforceable rights — they were the Republic’s conscience. They were written for governments, not courts. They were meant to whisper in the ear of every future leader: Build a just society. Build a humane society. Honour the poor.
And they would do exactly that. In later years, courts would interpret them expansively, Parliament would legislate in their direction, and governments would use them to justify transformative social policies.
But on that November day in 1948, they were still just words — fragile, hopeful, and deeply human.
The Assembly adopted them not because they were perfect, but because India needed dreams written into its Constitution. India needed a moral horizon.
And in that moment, the framers gave the nation one.
The Citizenship Debate — When Partition’s Wounds Burst Into the Assembly and Nehru Lost His Temper#On 10 August 1949, the Constituent Assembly faced one of the most emotionally charged debates in its entire tenure: citizenship. Until then, the Assembly had debated with passion, yes — but mostly with composure. That day, however, was different. Partition still haunted the country. Refugee camps overflowed in Delhi, Punjab, Bengal, and Assam. Families had been torn apart. Stories of violence traveled faster than trains. The pain was still raw, and citizenship — who belonged, who didn’t, who should be allowed back — became an explosive question.
The hall that morning felt unusually restless. Members shuffled papers, exchanged glances, and whispered anxiously. Everyone knew the debate would be difficult. India had just lived through a tragedy in which identity itself had become a matter of life and death. Now the Assembly had to decide who could call India home.
The debate opened with H. V. Kamath, who questioned the Draft Constitution’s relatively liberal provisions for those who had fled across the border. He argued that citizenship could not be granted
automatically to people who had “migrated” to Pakistan after Partition and then returned. His suspicion reflected a fear shared by many in the northern provinces — that allowing returnees too easily might open the door for infiltration or exploitation by those whose loyalties were uncertain.
His tone was sharp. The emotion behind it was unmistakable: fear.
Soon after, Mahavir Tyagi rose, echoing similar worries. His voice trembled with anger as he described the suffering of Hindu and Sikh refugees who had lost everything — homes, relatives, entire histories. Tyagi asked, in frustration, why the Constitution was so generous toward Muslims who had chosen to go to Pakistan but then wanted to return. “What about those who stayed and suffered here?” he demanded. His words were not polished, but they were honest. It was the honesty of someone still grieving.
The debate began drifting toward a dangerous edge. Some members framed their arguments in ways that carried communal undertones. Others grew defensive. Several speeches were interrupted. The pain of Partition had entered the chamber like a storm.
Then Jawaharlal Nehru, who had been listening quietly with a tightening jaw, rose to speak.
Nehru was not usually angry in the Assembly. When he disagreed, he did so gently, through persuasion rather than confrontation. But that day, something broke. As he rose, the silence in the hall shifted sharply. Members sensed a rare moment approaching.
Nehru began by saying that the Constitution could not be written based on fear or revenge. His voice was calm at first, but the emotion underneath it boiled quickly to the surface. He reminded the House that millions of innocents had suffered — Hindus, Muslims, Sikhs. Pain did not belong to one community. And the Constitution could not discriminate between citizens based on their religion or the chaos of circumstance.
Then his tone transformed. For perhaps the only time in the entire Assembly’s recorded history, Nehru directly chastised his colleagues. He accused some speakers of bringing “bitterness” and “narrow-mindedness” into the Constitution. His voice sharpened as he said: “We cannot have a Constitution that is based on fear and hatred.” He insisted that India was not Pakistan’s mirror image. India would not define citizenship based on religious identity.
Members stared at him, stunned. Nehru’s rare flash of anger was not theatrical. It came from deep pain
— the pain of watching a country he loved being torn apart by the same divisions that had caused Partition. He feared those divisions were creeping into the Constitution itself.
After a pause, he spoke more softly, but with even greater weight. He said that citizenship must be rooted in equality, humanity, and compassion. The Constitution must not punish people for the circumstances of their flight or return. If individuals had left India out of fear or confusion and wanted to return, they must not be treated as traitors unless there was clear cause. The republic must be generous, not vindictive.
His words did something remarkable. The anger in the room slowly dissipated. Members who had spoken with sharpness fell quiet. Several looked down at their desks. Nehru had not scolded them as individuals. He had reminded them of who they were, and what kind of country they were trying to build.
The debate continued, but the tone had been transformed. B. R. Ambedkar rose shortly afterward and defended the citizenship provisions with precision. He clarified that the rules were not lax; they were humane. People would have to prove residence, intention to stay, and lawful return. The clauses were structured, not sentimental. Ambedkar’s calm constitutional reasoning balanced Nehru’s emotional force. Together, they anchored the debate.
By the end of the day, the Assembly adopted a citizenship framework that was neither harsh nor naive. It reflected the dignity of a country refusing to let the horrors of Partition define its future.
What makes this anecdote unforgettable is not just the legal debate. It is the human moment when Nehru — usually the calm architect of consensus — finally broke under the weight of grief and fear, and reminded the Assembly that the Constitution could not be written in the shadow of hatred.
He stood not as a Prime Minister, but as a man refusing to let India become small-hearted.
On that August day in 1949, the Assembly remembered that a republic is not built by drawing lines around who belongs, but by opening a door and saying: “You may come home.”
The Oath Controversy — When the Assembly Debated Whether Officials Could Swear Allegiance Without Using the Word “God”#On 31 December 1948, the Constituent Assembly gathered to discuss something that might sound small on paper, but in that moment carried immense symbolic weight: the oath to be sworn by the President, Ministers, Members of Parliament, judges, and public servants. Few expected this to be a contentious day. But what unfolded was one of the Assembly’s most revealing debates — a moment
when India confronted the question of faith, conscience, and the freedom to affirm loyalty to the Republic without invoking a deity.
The hall that winter afternoon had the unhurried quiet of a year drawing to a close. Yet beneath the calm, a debate simmered about what an oath in a secular republic should look like. The Draft Constitution, drawing from older traditions, contained references to “solemnly swear in the name of God.” Many assumed this was harmless tradition. But others felt a deep discomfort.
The first to rise with a firm objection was K. M. Munshi, a devout man personally, but a fierce constitutional secularist. He argued that the oath of office in a modern Republic could not compel anyone to invoke God. The state must respect both belief and unbelief. His tone was gentle yet firm as he explained that an atheist, an agnostic, or someone whose faith structure did not include a single deity should not be forced to utter what they did not believe. A Constitution, he said, should never compel spiritual dishonesty.
As soon as Munshi finished, murmurs rose across the hall. Some members nodded in agreement. Others frowned, unsettled. The issue seemed simple, but it was not. India was a land of deep religiosity. The overwhelming majority of people invoked God reflexively in their public and private lives. Removing God from the oath, some felt, would strip the moment of its moral gravity.
That concern was voiced next, in a quiet but unmistakably emotional speech by Pandit Thakur Das Bhargava. He argued that an oath without God lacked the solemnity needed for high office. The invocation of God, he said, reminded individuals that they answered not merely to law, but to a higher moral order. His voice trembled slightly as he insisted that the phrase carried not sectarian meaning, but universal human seriousness.
The debate intensified. Members were not arguing about theology. They were arguing about what it meant to bind oneself to the Constitution — and whether that bond must pass through the language of divinity.
It was at this point that H. V. Kamath rose with an intervention that pushed the debate into sharper focus. Kamath, deeply spiritual yet intellectually uncompromising, argued that references to God should remain, but they should be broad enough to accommodate every faith tradition, including the possibility of refusing the reference. He suggested optional formulations — those who wished could swear, those who did not could affirm.
His suggestion eased the tension, but the debate still teetered between tradition and secularism.
Then the room shifted its attention to B. R. Ambedkar.
Ambedkar rose, carrying the calm authority that often settled the Assembly. He began by reminding members that the Constitution was being written for a secular democratic republic. The oath, he said, must reflect the spirit of that republic. No citizen could be forced to invoke God, nor could anyone be prevented from doing so.
Ambedkar argued that the oath must speak in the language of the Constitution, not the language of a particular religious tradition. He said something that captured the heart of the argument: the Constitution must secure freedom of conscience, and that freedom must begin at the very moment when one assumes constitutional office.
If the oath violated conscience, he said, the Constitution would violate itself at its own doorstep.
His reasoning was crisp, yet humane. The oath must be solemn, yes — but solemnity must come from sincerity, not compulsion.
Ambedkar proposed a solution that would become a hallmark of India’s secular character: every officeholder would have the option to either swear in the name of God or solemnly affirm without invoking God at all. The choice would belong entirely to the individual.
This simple compromise changed the debate instantly.
Members who had feared the abandonment of spiritual seriousness now saw that faith was being respected — not imposed. Members who had feared religious compulsion saw that conscience was being protected. The oath would honour belief and unbelief equally. It would be solemn without being sectarian, personal without being exclusionary.
When the clause was adopted, there was no sense of victory or defeat. Only the quiet satisfaction of having found a path that reflected the country’s deepest ethos: that the Republic belonged to everyone
— the devout, the doubting, and the unbelieving alike.
What makes this anecdote so meaningful is that it reveals the framers’ instinct for balance. In a room full of believers, the Assembly still defended the right not to invoke God. In a country steeped in religious tradition, they still chose a secular oath. And they did so not out of hostility to religion, but out of respect for conscience.
On that cold December afternoon, the Assembly ensured that every person who takes office in India would be bound by truth, not forced into ritual; by duty, not by dogma; by conscience, not compulsion.
It was a small debate with a large soul.
The Emergency Powers Debate — When the Assembly Warned Future India Not to Lose Its Soul#On 1G October 1949, the Constituent Assembly entered one of the darkest and most delicate debates it would ever face: the question of Emergency powers. Until then, the Assembly had argued passionately but hopefully about rights, federalism, and justice. But this debate forced them to imagine something far more unsettling — a moment when democracy itself could be suspended.
As the session opened, the hall felt uneasy. Members shifted in their seats, papers rustled nervously. Everyone understood what was at stake. Emergency powers were necessary — no one doubted that. India was a young nation, still healing from Partition, facing communal tensions, princely state integration issues, border uncertainties, and the global shadows of war and authoritarianism. But they also knew that extraordinary powers were dangerous even in the hands of the well-intentioned.
The first person to give voice to this fear was H. V. Kamath, and his words cut sharply through the room. He reminded the Assembly that the British had governed India using emergency-like powers to crush protests, imprison dissenters, and rule without accountability. Now, in free India, he worried that the Constitution might hand similar tools to future governments. His tone was not accusatory, but almost pleading — asking the House to remember the chains they had only recently broken.
Then Pandit Hirday Nath Kunzru, always measured and dignified, rose to speak. His voice carried a moral gravity that the Assembly never ignored. Emergency powers, he said, should be used only when the nation faced true danger — not when a government simply found criticism inconvenient or dissent annoying. He warned that if the Constitution allowed the executive to declare emergencies too easily, India could drift into authoritarianism without even noticing it. The frailty of democracies, especially new ones, was something he had studied deeply. His warning came not from fear, but from wisdom.
As Kunzru sat down, a heavy silence settled over the chamber. It was the silence of memory. Many members in that hall had lived through arrests, censorship, detention without trial, and the silencing of newspapers. They could not forget how emergency powers had been turned against them. Even those
who trusted independent India’s first leaders knew that the Constitution had to outlive personalities. It had to protect future citizens from future rulers.
The debate intensified when T. T. Krishnamachari took the floor. He agreed that emergency powers were dangerous. But in a voice both sober and pragmatic, he argued that the State must have the means to defend itself in times of real peril. India faced threats unknown to older nations — internal divisions, economic fragility, unsettled borders. Without strong emergency provisions, he said, the Constitution risked leaving the nation defenceless. His argument did not dismiss the fears of others; it acknowledged them, but insisted that courage also required preparedness.
The House listened, torn between two instincts — the instinct for liberty and the instinct for survival.
It was then that B. R. Ambedkar rose with a deliberateness that always quieted the room. He had crafted the emergency provisions with immense caution, and now he carried that same caution into his defence of them.
His voice was steady, but the words revealed an internal struggle. He acknowledged that Emergency powers were “fraught with danger,” that they could be misused, and that the Constitution must guard against that misuse. But he also insisted that India could not pretend the world was safe. He reminded the Assembly of invasions, insurrections, famines, and breakdowns of order that could threaten the very existence of the Republic.
Ambedkar explained that the Constitution tried to strike the narrowest possible balance:
Emergency powers would be allowed — but they would be limited, reviewable, and subject to parliamentary control. The President could act only on the advice of the Cabinet. The Emergency would need approval from Parliament. Rights could be suspended, yes, but only during grave crises.
Then he said something that echoed far beyond the walls of the Assembly: “The safeguards are sufficient only if the people remain vigilant.” It was a reminder that no constitutional clause, no matter how carefully crafted, could substitute for democratic culture.
After Ambedkar spoke, the Assembly fell into a long, contemplative silence. Members knew they were not writing provisions for ordinary times. They were writing for the worst of times — times when the country might be afraid, when the executive might be tempted, when the public might be silent. They were writing for moments when the Republic’s soul could be tested.
By the end of the day, the emergency provisions — what would become Articles 352 to 3G0 — were adopted. There was no jubilation. No applause. Only a sombre recognition that the Constitution had embraced a necessary danger.
What makes this anecdote so haunting is what came later. In 1975, the Emergency would be declared misusing precisely the powers the Assembly had feared. Rights would be suspended, dissent crushed, and democracy throttled. And Ambedkar’s warning — that safeguards mattered only when the people remained vigilant — would prove tragically prophetic.
But none of that was visible on that October day in 1949. All that was visible was a room full of men and women trying, with deep sincerity, to build a shield strong enough to protect India, yet fragile enough to preserve liberty.
The emergency debate revealed something essential about the framers: they were not naïve optimists. They understood power. They understood danger. And they understood that the Constitution could not save the Republic alone — the Republic would have to save the Constitution too.
Hansa Mehta and the Fight for Gender-Neutral Equality — In India and Across the World#Long before Hansa Jivraj Mehta walked into the Constituent Assembly of India, she had already etched her name into global constitutional history. In 1947–48, she served as India’s representative on the United Nations Human Rights Commission, working directly with Eleanor Roosevelt during the drafting of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR). According to UN drafting records and the Eleanor Roosevelt Papers, the first article of the draft UDHR originally read, “All men are born free and equal.” Many delegates saw nothing unusual in this phrasing — it was formulaic, inherited from older charters. But Hansa Mehta refused to let the phrase stand (United Nations Archives; Eleanor Roosevelt Papers Project).
She argued — firmly and repeatedly — that using “men” would erase women from the very document meant to enshrine universal dignity. As The Better India’s documented account of the UDHR drafting explains, Mehta pressed the Commission to adopt truly inclusive language, insisting that rights belong to all human beings, not merely “men.” Eleanor Roosevelt supported her, and the Commission eventually accepted her amendment (The Better India, “How Hansa Mehta Changed the UDHR”). The final text of Article 1 now reads:
“All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.”
This victory shaped the way the entire world talked about equality. And it was this clarity about the power of language that Hansa carried with her when she took her seat in India’s constitution-making chamber.
Inside the Constituent Assembly, her interventions were never loud or confrontational, but they were precise. The Assembly was still wrestling with the aftermath of Partition, the challenge of forging a new federal structure, and the balancing of minority rights. Amid these vast questions, gender equality could easily have been overshadowed. Yet Hansa ensured it never was.
One of the most revealing moments came when the Assembly debated whether Muslim women should have separate electorates or special political arrangements. On the surface, the proposal seemed protective. But Hansa saw its deeper implications. Drawing on her experience as a women’s rights activist, she argued that separate electorates would not empower women; they would isolate them. In the Constituent Assembly Debates, she reminded members that women’s organisations across India had not asked for reserved electorates or special political categories. What they wanted — and what they had consistently demanded — was equality.
Speaking on 22 November 1948, she declared that women were not seeking “special privileges.” Instead, they sought “social justice, economic justice and political justice… equality which can alone be the basis of mutual respect” (Constituent Assembly Debates, 22–23 November 1948; also analysed in Verfassungsblog, “The Women Behind India’s Constitution”). This was not a rejection of women’s political participation. It was a rejection of political segregation.
Her argument carried weight. India’s women had marched in the freedom struggle, endured imprisonment, and fought side by side with men — and they had not asked for political silos. To give them separate electorates after Independence, she warned, would turn them into political dependents. The Assembly listened. Slowly, support for separate electorates vanished.
Beyond specific proposals, Hansa Mehta shaped the very language of the Constitution. Whenever draft clauses used masculine pronouns or formulations that could be interpreted as male-specific, she intervened. Scholars like Rohit De and Danielle Khan in Verfassungsblog note that she pushed repeatedly for gender-neutral terminology, ensuring that “citizens” meant both women and men in every constitutional context. Her insistence mirrored her battle at the United Nations: equality begins with the words that define the human being.
What makes Hansa’s work in the Assembly remarkable is that she operated in a chamber overwhelmingly male, at a time when women in politics were still fighting for recognition. Yet she did not seek symbolic gestures or special concessions. Instead, she demanded equal citizenship — rooted in rights, not reservations; in language, not leniency.
Her influence was quiet but transformative. Because of her interventions, India’s Constitution speaks in a voice that includes women not as an exception, but as an intrinsic part of its imagination. She ensured that the Republic’s foundational text did not slip into linguistic habits that echoed centuries of exclusion.
Looking back, her legacy beautifully intertwines two achievements: she changed the language of human rights for the world by transforming the UDHR (“All human beings…”), and she changed the language of citizenship for India by insisting that gender equality be woven into every principle of the Constitution. Her work reminds us that revolutions often begin not with grand declarations, but with carefully chosen words — words that ensure no one is forgotten.

title: Indian Young Lawyers Association vs The State of Kerala
content:
INDIAN YOUNG LAWYERS ASSOCIATION VERSUS THE STATE OF KERALA#[Indian Young Lawyers Association versus the State of Kerala]{.underline} is a 2018 case related to the entry of women aged between 10 and 50 into the Sabrimala Temple in Kerala. The entry of women into the temple was prohibited on the grounds of purity and sanctity and thus was considered discriminatory in nature. The writ petition was filed first in the Kerala High Court, where the decision came in favour of the prohibition. A group of five women lawyers then went to the Supreme Court against the judgment of the Kerala High Court. The petitioners
argued that the prohibition violates the Fundamental Rights of women enshrined in Articles 14, 15, 17 and 25.
The Sabrimala Temple is situated in the Sabrimala hills in the state of Kerala. The temple is [dedicated to Lord Ayappa]{.underline}, who is considered to have been born out of the Union of Lord
Shiva and Lord Vishnu in his Mohini avtar. The Ayappa is widely worshipped, especially in the Southern part of India. However, the Sabrimala Temple is the most prominent due to its story of divine origin. It is believed that Lord Ayappa himself directed King Rajsekara to build a temple here at the Sabrimala hills. It is also said that Lord Ayappa himself advised about the practice of pilgrimage and penance, or Vratham, to be followed for the pilgrimage to the temple. Vratham is a form of rigorous penance to be performed for 41 days by the person who wishes to offer a pilgrimage to the Sabrimala Temple. The devotee has to follow the rules like cooking their own food, staying away from family, abstaining from physical relations, etc. These all rules were aimed at the mental and physical purity of the devotee.
The women cannot perform the practice of Vratham for 41 days, as they have to go through menstruation, and thus, their entry was prohibited in the temple to maintain the purity of the Temple. Another argument in favour of prohibition was that Lord Ayappa, in this temple, resides as Naistika Brahmachari, meaning lifelong celibate. The women's pilgrimage to the temple could result in disturbing the celibacy of Lord Ayappa.
This prohibition was the root cause of the filing of the writ petition. The petitioners argued that such a prohibition on the entry of women is unconstitutional. Article 14, which guarantees equal protection under the law, was invoked by the petitioners. Additionally, the practice violates Article 15 as it discriminates based on sex, as well as breaches Article 17 by promoting untouchability through the notion of women being impure. Article 25 of the Constitution provides freedom to practice and propagate religion. The article gives power to practice essential religious practices in which the state cannot interfere. However, the petitioners argued that the exclusion of women from entering is not part of essential religious practices. The practice is only 60 years old and thus is not essential in character. It was also
argued that the Sabrimala Temple is not a separate religious denomination but part of Hinduism and thus cannot restrict women from entering the premises.
Question of Law#1 AIR 2018 SUPREME COURT 1650
The major Question of Law was whether the prohibition on the entry of women promotes discrimination based on sex, as well as untouchability, thus violating Articles 15 and 17. The Court also contended on the issue of whether the entry in the temple forms the basis of essential religious practices protected under Article 25. Deliberations were also made regarding the scope of Article 26. The article provides religious denominations with the freedom to manage religious affairs. The Question of Law was raised whether a religious institution can exercise exclusionary power in the name of management. The denominational character of the Sabrimala Temple was also contested. Section 3(b) of Kerala Hindu Worship (Authorisation of Entry) Rules, 1965 states that women who, by custom and usage, are not allowed to enter the temple should not be allowed to enter for worship. The question was also in front of the bench whether this Section is constitutional or not.
Judgment#The court, in its judgment, held that the practice of prohibiting women from entering into the Sabrimala Temple is constitutional and is not consistent with Articles 14, 15 and 17. The court also held that the Sabrimala Temple is not a religious denomination in itself but part of Hinduism, and thus, entry cannot be restricted. The court also concluded that the prohibition of entry is not a part of essential religious practices. The restriction on the entry based on the menstrual cycle was considered unethical and a promotion of untouchability and inequality by the court. The court also invalidated Section 3(b) as it hindered the freedom of women to practice religion
A review petition was filed instantly after the Judgment was delivered. A nine-judge bench was formed for the hearing, and currently it is still in the Court.
References#Indian Young Lawyers Association versus the State of Kerala AIR 2018 SUPREME COURT 1650
